articles.title: Don’t Mourn Hakeem Jeffries’s Speakership. Organize.
articles.author: Austin Warrington
articles.content: In the wake of the midterms, the entirety of left-liberal America was jubilant. Democrats won majorities in the House and Senate, outperforming even the most idealistic predictions. But it was not only the Democratic victories that shocked observers — it was the kind of candidates who won. Democratic socialists had their strongest showing of any election in recent history, winning 169 endorsed ballot measures and seats at the local, state, and federal levels — their strongest showing of any general election in recent history. And the wins by nonsocialist progressives and even many centrists affirmed an agenda championed by democratic socialists, centering economic populism, wealth redistribution, and universal health care. But then a harsh reality set in: the near inevitability of Rep. Hakeem Jeffries as the next Speaker of the House, a result that seemed to fly in the face of the progressive results we’d just seen. On Wednesday, just eleven Democrats voted against Jeffries in an internal nonbinding vote, including a bloc of five newly elected democratic socialists, joined by two additional Democrats. In a statement on their decision, the no voters cited ongoing negotiations around “Medicare for All, stopping [Immigration and Customs Enforcment (ICE)] terror, getting money out of politics, [and] ending the genocide in Gaza.” Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez notably did not join the no votes. Jeffries is decidedly not a leftist nor a progressive. He is a pro-corporate Democrat who defends Israel and readily takes American Israel Public Affairs Committee money and corporate money. How, in the face of such a resounding progressive message from voters, could there be no clear alternative? It’s understandable that some on the Left might feel deflated by this outcome. But we can also see the speaker conundrum as exposing an organizing void in Congress, one that the broadly left-leaning forces that felt so heartened by the midterm results have to confront soberly: we simply do not currently have the power, leverage, or internal relationships to elect a speaker that reflects the mandate we just witnessed. Changing that reality will need to start with an honest evaluation of the conditions surrounding the speakership race. Jeffries has spent years building up to this moment. The relationships he’s nurtured with his careful, deliberate style and results he’s delivered to the Democratic caucus — negotiating important earmarks for Democrats in a Republican-controlled House, leading a multistate campaign to neutralize Republicans’ gerrymandering efforts, and steering increasingly large fundraising hauls to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee — were all leading to this moment. Any challenger, particularly one from a rising Left that is at its very beginnings in the halls of power, would be at a massive disadvantage. Not only that, but any defectors willing to stick their necks out to back an alternative would be putting a target on their back, as Jeffries plays a key role in committee assignments and setting the agenda for the floor. Asking our electeds to risk their ability to successfully carry out their jobs and advance our priorities would be irresponsible without a viable path to success. Socialists grappling with increasing power in government have to think long-term about how to create the conditions where a majority of House Democrats can back a socialist speaker. The time to start building toward that outcome is now, in Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) working groups and organizing committees across the country. Our bench of socialist electeds needs to be deeper in a way that can build buy-in for our goals among the general public, and we need to continue the work of relationship-building with our existing socialist electeds. Deepening our bench of electeds happens at every level of government and requires a clear-eyed assessment of what it takes to win races, which usually centers on an ambitious fundraising plan. Designated candidate recruitment organizers can begin by identifying prospective candidates and taking meetings now in anticipation of 2028; ideal candidates have preexisting ties to DSA or a labor union, direct organizing experience, a demonstrated commitment to advancing socialist policies, and a willingness to work collaboratively and meet regularly with chapter leaders once elected. Creating buy-in and demonstrating the popularity of our agenda among the public requires frequent and honest communication with the public. Rep. Ocasio-Cortez excels at this, making the often opaque operations of Congress accessible to millions through social media. To elect a socialist speaker, we would need to launch a campaign early, educating the public on the mechanisms as well as the stakes of the speaker’s race and building consensus around a candidate. A successful campaign will put us in a strong position when it is time for members to vote, where we can flex our organizing muscle to exert pressure using all of the support we’ve built throughout the course of the campaign. Most importantly, we will need to continue the work of building relationships with our bloc of socialist electeds across the country. This work is carried out by trusted organizing leaders in regularly scheduled group meetings . It necessitates strong interpersonal skills on both ends, including the ability to manage conflict healthily and negotiate. Chapters with maturing socialist coalitions should connect with the architects of more established programs to take some of the many lessons that have emerged over the years. What distinguishes democratic socialists from other politicians is that strategizing and organizing don’t stop after election day. The project of building power is year-round and relies on the active participation of skilled organizers working with elected officials. In the past two weeks, Representatives-elect Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier have organized canvasses of their constituents, asking them directly what they should prioritize in Congress and who they should back as speaker. This ongoing dialogue with constituents represents a new kind of strategy — one in which elected officials meet people where they’re at to continue the work of organizing outside of an electoral context, facilitating dialogue at the doors and creating trust and buy-in. This is only a small piece of what it will take to win our agenda, but it is an important and meaningful step toward the kind of politics we should always be practicing: one that centers the needs of working people and ensures their voices echo in the halls of power. articles.title: Anthropic Is Already Part of the Security Establishment
articles.author: Jacob Davis
articles.content: Anthropic, which priced its initial public offering (IPO) last night and began trading on the Nasdaq today, published an S-1, the corporate prospectus for the offering. The document, which extends over five hundred pages, is intended to provide potential investors with an outline of its corporate structure, business model, and financial situation. Much of the document is, accordingly, dedicated to mundane legal minutiae: long lists of hypothetical events that might adversely affect investments, specific provisions for investment to comply with foreign nations’ securities law, etc. Some points, however, are quite instructive. As the filing explains, large-scale corporate decisions are overseen by a “long-term benefit trust” (LTBT): a five-person body responsible for appointing a majority of Anthropic’s board and entitled to a special class of corporate stock. Unlike most benefit trusts, the LTBT is a “‘ purpose trust ’ that is managed for the achievement of a purpose rather than for the benefit of a particular set of beneficiaries.” While the LTBT itself has received mainstream attention , less notice has been given to the identity of the trustees. Of the four currently appointed, one is Ben Bernanke — infamous as the architect of the Obama-era Wall St bailouts. And one is Richard Fontaine, chief executive officer of the Center for a New American Security ( CNAS ) and North American executive director of the Trilateral Commission . The latter appointment is especially noteworthy, for it speaks to an increasing coalescence of Anthropic, effective altruism, and the US national security establishment. Company Purpose The LTBT is something of a novelty in corporate structure. It is a fine-tuning of the usual public benefit corporation (PBC) — a form of corporate governance that allows the company to balance other stated interests against the pecuniary interests of its shareholders. Anthropic’s innovation is to hand over much of the responsibility of enforcing these competing interests to the LTBT, which will eventually appoint a majority of the board of directors. The company is also unusual in the sweeping humanitarian nature of its “company purpose,” against which shareholder returns are to be balanced: “the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity.” The LTBT is an important indicator of Anthropic’s ethical self-understanding. According to the S-1, it “is intended to operate as an independent body of Trustees with expertise in AI safety, national security, public policy, and social enterprise.” These experts are selected for their perceived competence in promoting the humanitarian company purpose and “the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct” — a class which, given Anthropic’s stated beliefs about its potential impact, includes all living humans. In addition to vesting them with material power, therefore, Anthropic’s choice of LTBT members says something about what the company understands those humanitarian interests to be. A Greater Degree of Moderation in Democracy Both CNAS and the Trilateral Commission enjoy a dark reputation among critics of the US-aligned international security community. The commission is especially notorious, and has long starred as the villain in a number of conspiracy theories of varying levels of plausibility. CNAS, however, may yet be the more influential of the two, and is to all appearances more bound up with the emerging hybrid of corporate AI, effective altruism, and the security establishment. The Trilateral Commission is a private, international membership organization intended “to discuss and propose solutions to some of the world’s toughest problems.” Members include various senior government officials, business executives, and academics. They are drawn primarily from the commission’s eponymous three regional groups: Europe (mainly Western), East Asia (mainly Japan), and North America (mainly the United States). Their official 2025 leadership list , which names Fontaine as executive director of the North American group, mourns the passing of two founders: David Rockefeller and Dr Henry Kissinger. The commission’s operations are famously clandestine, which together with the elite status of many of its members has contributed to its perennial mystique. Among leftists, it may be best known for its 1975 report (one of only a handful available to the public), “The Crisis of Democracy” — which was prominently criticized at the time by Noam Chomsky. The report’s section on the United States, authored by conservative intellectual Samuel P. Huntington, ascribes the preceding decade’s social turmoil to an “excess of democracy” — to be counteracted by “a greater degree of moderation in democracy.” Included in this excess were protest movements opposed to the Vietnam War and in support of racial justice. These movements helped dangerously integrate hitherto marginal populations, like black Americans, into the political process. “This marginality on the part of some groups [ . . . has] been one of the factors which has enabled democracy to function effectively.” Half a century later, a similar attitude toward protest survives in Anthropic’s commercial and political activities. As Daniel Boguslaw details in The American Prospect , the company has been explicit about its plans to deploy AI to surveil, predict, and stifle protest activism. These plans include collaboration with law enforcement, and fit well with historical calls for digital surveillance from AI safety lobbyists at organizations with ties to Anthropic. Fontaine, who has served as the commission’s North American executive director since 2019, was appointed to Anthropic’s LTBT in 2025. The Revolving Door CNAS, on the other hand, is a Washington-based national security think tank with extensive ties to both Republican and Democratic White House administrations. Joe Biden and Donald Trump staffers with CNAS ties include senior figures like Avery Alpha , who occupied high-level roles at the Central Intelligence Agency and Department of Homeland Security from 2017 to 2025 before turning to consultancy work. The organization has traditionally pursued a broadly neoconservative line on foreign policy. Fontaine was elevated as president in 2012, only to be promoted again to CEO in 2019 — five months before his Trilateral Commission executive appointment. CNAS also has an exceptional history of conflicts of interest and likely illicit influence. Several of these came to light in a 2021 bombshell report by the Revolving Door Project, which also helped expose CNAS members’ deep presence in the Biden and Trump administrations. The center has repeatedly championed private sector industries, international organizations, and foreign governments from whom it has received funding — often without explicit acknowledgement in the course of their advocacy. Fontaine himself has taken direct part in these ethically suspect lobbying campaigns. In 2009, for example, he coauthored a policy paper defending the use of private military contractors in the war on terror — without any explicit acknowledgement of CNAS’s funding from several military contractor firms. He also did not acknowledge the $25,000–$50,000 funding the think tank had received from the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, during an event to promote NATO in 2019 at the Truman Library. Anthropic is now itself among the beneficiaries of this conflict-ridden advocacy. On November 3, CNAS published a report advocating a suite of policy recommendations to protect against autonomous AI agents. The proposed policies align largely with Anthropic’s own stated regulatory agenda. And, conspicuously, certain of the policies clearly serve Anthropic’s commercial interests — especially against Chinese competitors. These include crackdowns on potential avenues of model distillation by foreign entities as well as diplomacy to erect barriers to powerful open-weights models. Model distillation by Chinese competitors has long been a sore point for Anthropic, and these competitors overwhelmingly favor open-weights licensing. At no point does the report mention Fontaine’s ties to Anthropic. This hidden connection is just one part of a broader integration of CNAS, Anthropic, and affiliated organizations. CNAS affiliates now include major figures at Anthropic, like the center’s adjunct senior fellow, Michael Sellitto . Sellitto, who served on the National Security Council during the Obama and first Trump administrations and currently serves on the Council for Foreign Relations, is head of Anthropic’s Global Affairs team. The team is associated with Anthropic’s known surveillance activities and advocacy. Effective Altruists and New Cold Warriors CNAS has also maintained a partnership with the Center for Security and Emerging Technology (CSET) — an Anthropic-linked AI safety lobbying organization with deep ties in Washington. In 2025, for example, CSET announced its new advisory board, including CNAS member Michael Brown . It has also collaborated on several policy documents and research projects, particularly on combating Chinese AI development . CSET enjoys extensive connections with Anthropic. These include personal overlaps, like Anthropic adviser and CSET Senior Fellow Ben Buchanan, or Anthropic policy executive and CSET advisory board member Joel Meyer . The two organizations have collaborated on the CHIPS Act and export controls against China, and are generally united under the ideological banner of effective altruism and AI safety. In addition to personnel, CSET, CNAS, and Anthropic are linked financially through Coefficient Giving, the premier effective altruist donor body. Since its founding in 2019, CSET has received over $100 million from Coefficient Giving (formerly Open Philanthropy), most of it in advance of its collaboration with CNAS. CNAS, too, has received funding directly from Coefficient Giving, albeit in smaller quantities. The bulk of this transfer was conducted in 2022 and 2025, when it received grants of a bit over $5 million and $8 million, respectively, for work in AI governance and security. These larger grants built on a series of smaller ones (from around $24,000 to $260,000) starting in 2017. Anthropic enjoys deep ideological and personal ties with Coefficient Giving. Both emerged from the effective altruist and AI safety movements, which continue to shape their rhetoric and policy directions. Holden Karnofsky, cofounder of Coefficient Giving’s precursor GiveWell, is married to Anthropic board member Daniela Amodei, herself the sister of Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. Neil Shah , another LTBT member, served as managing director of Givewell until 2022. And Joe Carlsmith formerly led the AI-focussed “Worldview Investigations” team at Coefficient Giving (then Open Philanthropy). Now, he heads the “character” team at Anthropic, which is devoted to tailoring the values and personality of the company’s “Claude” assistants. In the coming years and months, we are likely to witness a new influx of Anthropic money into Coefficient Giving and similar funding organizations — and thereby to more distant beneficiaries like CSET and CNAS. Many employees and executives have announced their intention to donate large portions of their wealth to charity, sometimes up to 80 percent. Coefficient Giving, itself a tax-deductible 501(c)3 nonprofit , has been recognized as a “ favorite ” of Anthropic executives, whose personal net worths extend into the tens of billions. In addition to laundering the donors’ reputations, these wealth transfers thus promise to further entrench the financial and organizational ties between Anthropic on the one hand and the Washington security establishment on the other. Entanglement The foregoing connections only scratch the surface of Anthropic’s ever-deepening entanglement with the security state. Beyond Fontaine, for example, the LTBT includes Harvard physicist Christopher Stubbs — who in addition to his academic appointments serves as a member of the independent scientific advisory group JASON. JASON’s work (much of it classified) largely concentrates on defense and nuclear strategy, including “studies under contract to the Department of Defense, the Department of Energy, the National Nuclear Security Administration, the U.S. Intelligence Community, and the FBI.” Most notoriously, it collaborated with military leadership during the Vietnam War, as revealed by Freedom of Information Act disclosures in 2002. These connections do not merely speak to the increasing influence of the security establishment over Anthropic (and vice versa). They are also a clue as to the meaning of the company’s professed concern for human welfare and survival. Together with statements from company leadership, they paint a picture of long-term human interests deeply inflected by interventionist, antidemocratic, and anti-privacy strains in modern American foreign policy. Those who distrust such strains would do well to regard Anthropic, or any company with similar entanglements, with serious apprehension. articles.title: The Health Insurance Experience
articles.author: Rochester Red Star: News from Rochester DSA
articles.content: by Sara C The following text is adapted from a speech delivered by Sara C at the NY Health Act Rally held October 17 at Rochester’s Liberty Pole. Despite health insurance being the primary way most Americans access any kind of health care, it’s not exactly popular. It can be expensive, not just in the premiums we pay for it with every paycheck, but also with deductibles that mean coverage doesn’t even start until you’ve paid a certain amount out of pocket. The coverage itself can be frustratingly limited. Beyond all that, health insurance companies have plenty of tactics to avoid payment and accountability. This is my story of fighting against health insurance companies’ duplicitous practices, what I’ve learned from it, and what I see as a potential (if partial) solution. I was diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes when I was 8 years old. I will need insulin injections or infusions for the rest of my life to stay alive, because my body is incapable of making its own. There is no cure for type 1 diabetes at this point in time, and there is no way to treat it without insulin. Like many chronic illnesses, treatment plans vary from person to person. Some diabetics do better on injections and some do better on insulin pumps. Among pump users, different pumps address different needs that people have. Endocrinologists generally agree that finding the right system for the individual increases length and quality of life, which is generally the goal of medicine! In 2024, I started ordering pump supplies through a supply distribution company and billing it to my employer-funded insurance, who allegedly told the distributor that I was covered. Months later, I started getting bills for the full price of my pump supplies. I then spent two (2) years on the phone at least once a week with insurance and supply companies, submitting appeals and detailed information including letters from my doctor, only for the final result to be that they still refused to cover my pump supplies because they’re a “plan exception”. There was only one pump they covered, and it was one I had tried but hadn’t had success with. I’m lucky that I have generous friends and family who contributed to helping me pay out of pocket this past year, which came to about $2,000. That’s nothing to an insurance company. It’s unaffordable for me. I was so stressed about this that I started having chest pains. I had some tests done to make sure it was nothing more serious than anxiety and stress. (It wasn’t.) Unfortunately, I have a 10% co-insurance for such tests, and it turns out they’re very expensive, so I also owed over $500 for those. While I was dealing with this, I found out that the mammogram I got this February – because I have a family history of breast cancer – was also not covered because I was not yet 40. No exceptions for family history, and no exceptions for being only a few months short of 40. That was another $300 added to my medical payments and debt. I also pay about $50 a month in co-pays for my insulin, my continuous glucose monitor (CGM), and other medications. If that weren’t enough, I’m now getting immunotherapy injections so I can go outdoors in the summer without my eyes becoming unbearably itchy, which costs me $50 per week, a co-pay that is only $5 less than the full charge. I now have my pump supplies covered because I emailed my HR department, desperate, and gave them the intimate details of my medical needs. They had my pump and its supplies specifically added to the plan, two years after I had been fighting with the insurance company and all they had told me was no. Not one insurance rep suggested that I ask my company to add it to the plan. I shouldn’t have had to do any of that to get my medical needs met. The only reason health insurance companies exist is to generate profit by denying people care. That’s literally it. I suspect that “plan exceptions” will become more popular with insurance companies in the coming years, as a tactic to deny care and increase profits. I have also noticed that communication between patient and health insurance has become more and more opaque. When I asked for a list of “plan exceptions”, I was told that was not possible. Whether it didn’t exist, or the person I spoke to just didn’t have access to it, I don’t know. That’s another tactic: they set call center employees up with a script, don’t give them any more information than they give the patient, and limit their ability to escalate. They also don’t save notes about your case in a way that makes it easy for successive call center employees to access, so you have to fully explain why you’re calling every single time before you run into the brick wall of their inability to do anything about it. This makes calling to try and get something covered an enraging and Sisyphean task, and many people just give up and pay out of pocket. Many plans, like mine, also have medical and pharmacy coverage separated under different companies who don’t communicate with each other. While trying to get coverage for my pump supplies, my medical insurance told me it wasn’t covered by them as durable medical equipment (DME), so it should be covered under pharmacy, but when I called the pharmacy insurance, they said the opposite, sending me in circles with no accountability. This is not poor system design. This is how the system was fully intended to be designed so that executives and shareholders make as much money as possible. Private health insurance kills people in a myriad of ways: A lack of health insurance kills people. We’ve all heard the stories of diabetics like me who die because they lost insurance and can’t afford insulin. (I won’t go into details about how diabetic ketoacidosis is a horrible way to die, but trust me, it is.) Even people who do have health insurance die because their condition or its treatment isn’t covered and they can’t afford it. There are also the people who die by suicide rather than continue to fight tooth and nail just to survive every day. All of this is about to increase because of federal cuts. Scientists at UPenn predicted last year that Trump’s cuts could lead to 51,000 preventable deaths per year. Then, there are the people who survive but can’t thrive, because they can only access limited or less appropriate treatments. Or they are forced into poverty to pay for care. Doctors know that stress can have a severely negative impact on your health, so it’s hard to actually get healthy when you’re constantly fighting with insurance, or aren’t sure where your next meal or rent check is coming from. //Health insurance functions as a tool to keep working class people oppressed. One in four employed people in the U.S. stay at their job because they don’t want to lose health insurance, even though they would like to leave. Employers absolutely use this as a threat to keep workers in line. If you search on social media, you will see thousands of stories like mine, and even doctors advocating for their patients who were denied insurance coverage. It is abundantly clear that my insurance story is not a one-off, and not even particularly horrific, relatively speaking: I came through with no long-term negative health effects, no brushes with starvation or homelessness. Many Americans are not so lucky. So, what can we do? A great first step is to get the New York Health Act (NYHA) passed. This is a bill that has been floating in the state legislature for 35 years, and it would create a universal single-payer health care system in New York. It would be funded by a progressive income tax that is far, far lower than most of us are paying right now in premiums alone. Such a tax would have the wealthy paying their fair share to keep everyone in the state healthy. There would be no premiums, no co-payments, no co-insurance, no deductibles: all New York residents get full coverage and pay only the tax. It would eliminate the need for private health insurance: even health care while traveling interstate would be covered. (For more information, please see nyhcampaign.org .) Of course, there are many other problems in our healthcare system: for-profit hospitals and medical centers, leading to staff shortages; a for-profit pharmaceutical industry; medical racism, misogyny, fatphobia, and lots of other biases that affect care; and the fact that the lack of universal health care is a national problem, not just a state one. The NYHA wouldn’t solve all of our problems, but it would drastically improve – and save – the lives of so many New Yorkers. We have more than enough evidence that health insurance companies are killing and impoverishing us, deliberately. We need to band together and show that we don’t need them anymore. If you’re a union member, please push for your union to support the NYHA if it doesn’t already. Unions resistant to giving up the power of bargaining for health insurance have been one of the biggest blocks to passing it, but taking health insurance off the table will leave more room for unions to bargain for better pay, conditions, and other benefits. And please contact your state senator and assemblymember to let them know that you support the NYHA. May we have a future where no one needs to worry about things like premiums, deductibles, prior authorizations, and plan exceptions. articles.title: How Will We Get People to Work Under Socialism?
articles.author: Nick French
articles.content: With Zohran Mamdani’s rise to the mayoralty of the United States’s largest city and democratic socialists winning more and more elected offices at all levels across the country, there is renewed interest in and excitement about the idea of democratic socialism. But among socialists, there is little consensus on the content of that ideal. Many on the Left describe socialism in terms of greater income redistribution or an expanded public sector, with some socialists even describing their vision as compatible with capitalism. But we are seeing a growing number of proposals for feasible postcapitalist futures , distinct from both the social democratic welfare states and the state socialist systems of the twentieth century. In a recent article for Catalyst: A Journal of Theory and Strategy , Jacobin editor Nick French tackles the question of how a just postcapitalist society could get people to work. French argues that a just socialist society would recognize and enforce a general obligation to work while also protecting individual freedom; he argues that labor markets are the best institutional means to achieving these goals. Jacobin contributor Neal Meyer recently sat down with French to talk through the case for labor markets, including arguments against “postwork” visions of life after capitalism and appeals to moral motives, and what sort of economic inequalities might persist under socialism. You can listen to their conversation here . This transcript has been edited for length and clarity. The Duty to Work Neal Meyer We could start by talking about why you think people should work. It sounds like a preposterous question, but it actually is an important intervention. You and I are basically the same age; when we were in our twenties, the anarchist, libertarian left milieu was quite popular. I remember, as I was getting politicized, people talking about how people should have the right to be lazy, that we want to live in a postwork future. But in your article, you’re making an argument that people should work — that people have a duty to work. Nick French I’ll have something to say about these advocates of postwork socialism or postwork communism. But first, on the idea of a duty to work: it’s very intuitive to most people. In order to produce the things that we need, individually and collectively, we have to engage in labor. That often means doing things we don’t want to do, or spending our time such that we would rather be doing something else. It means exercising our capacities for particular ends to serve social needs. This is a kind of burden, a very significant burden, that is placed on people. My argument is trying to develop the intuitive idea that there are duties of fairness to other members of society. Insofar as you’re able to work — you’re not significantly disabled, or we can make accommodations for people to work — we all have an obligation to contribute to society through our labor. Maybe the more interesting questions about a duty to work are about how we might implement it. Also, people have a lot of objections to the idea that there’s a duty to work based around very valid worries, or even revulsion, at the way the work ethic is deployed in our capitalist society, which is brutally unjust. Oftentimes the reason people are not working is not because they don’t want to, or because they’re just lazy. It’s because they’re actually excluded from the labor market; there’s not enough work to go around. Or they’re not working because they haven’t been provided with adequate educational opportunities, or they’re sick or disabled, and so on. I’m not trying to make the argument that, in our actually existing society, people who aren’t working are immoral, or that we ought to shame people who are unemployed. Rather, the argument is: if we were to construct a fair society, where people have basic economic security, where everybody has equal access to high-quality education, where there are institutions that really do give everybody who can work a shot at getting a good job that pays well and treats them with dignity — in that ideal situation, we should expect everyone to contribute. Neal Meyer This is very much a conversation about the obligations we would have to each other in a future society, not our current society. Nick French Right. This is an argument in what philosophers sometimes call “ideal theory,” about the principles that would apply in a society that is basically just. Freedom of Occupational Choice Neal Meyer Part of the conception of justice you advance regarding labor is this idea that people should have a right to choose their occupation. Can you say more about that? And then, what’s the contrast you’re trying to draw here? Are there societies where that’s not the case? Nick French This is another idea that is intuitive to most people, but it’s important to articulate it clearly. Because when we start trying to come up with a detailed vision of what socialism might look like, it’s important as a North Star to block certain authoritarian possibilities. The idea of freedom of occupational choice is based in the notion that individual freedom, or autonomy, is an overriding value. This is something that’s common ground between the Marxist socialist tradition and the left-liberal philosophical tradition, chiefly as represented by people like John Stuart Mill and John Rawls, who I draw on a lot in this article. It’s very important that we be able to choose how we spend our time and how we exercise and develop our productive, creative, and intellectual capacities. Part of how we do that is with the traditional civil liberties: freedom of speech, freedom of movement, freedom of assembly, freedom of association, the kinds of things people are familiar with from the US Bill of Rights. But freedom of choice of occupation is really important too. In formulating an idea of how I want to live my life, I’m crucially thinking about how I want to contribute to society. What sort of productive capacities do I want to develop and exercise? Do I want to be an engineer or a mechanic, an artist or a writer? These are fundamental to people’s identities in contemporary society. And that’s a kind of liberty that we should hope a socialist society would not just preserve but maximize. When it comes to the potential contrasts or alternatives I have in mind, I’m thinking of societies where people are either prevented from taking on certain occupations or forced to take on certain jobs or occupations in an extensive way, where there’s not much room for people to set their own course in life. There’s formal legal discrimination, when employers discriminate openly on the basis of race or sex. That obviously is a major violation of freedom of choice of occupation. Again, most people in contemporary society would already reject such discrimination; the right to freedom of choice of occupation protects against it. But it also protects against a vision of a more coercive or Stalinist-style socialism, where you have a central authority assigning people to certain jobs because that’s where they are supposedly most needed. We should guard against that as well. Neal Meyer You mention in the article that that’s not even how state socialist societies actually handled the labor obligation problem. People had the freedom to choose their occupations to a large extent. Nick French That’s right. These societies did have what were called “parasite laws.” The constitutions of the Soviet Union and other state socialist countries enshrined a duty to work, and they had laws on the books that would criminalize not working. If you refused to work at all, you would be punished. But in general, they didn’t tell people they had to work in certain occupations. This is more of a theoretical possibility than something that was actually implemented on a large scale. Can a Basic Income Free Us From Work? Neal Meyer Your article sets up these goals and then walks through a couple of models that you disagree with before presenting your desired option. The first idea you criticize is what people will probably be most familiar with, which is the universal basic income (UBI). Nick French To be clear, I’m not arguing against UBI as a policy. I think something like a UBI would be an important part of a socialist institutional framework. What I’m arguing against is the idea that a UBI could free people from the need to work, which is how postwork theorists present it. People might still work out of the goodness of their hearts, or intrinsic joy in certain activities, but there would be no compulsion, or no duty or necessity, to work. Here I’m drawing on Alex Gourevitch, who had a great piece in Catalyst a few years ago arguing against this postwork idea at length. His basic thought is, if nobody’s working because everybody is just taking a UBI, then no one is producing the goods that people would buy with that UBI. So it’s a fantasy that the UBI could free people from having to work. One argument that some postwork thinkers emphasize is that automation can come in, the robots can come in, to do all the work that was formerly done by humans. That’s how we could have no one working and everyone just taking the UBI, because the machines are producing everything we need. I started working on this project before AI was at the top of everyone’s minds, and maybe now a lot of people think it’s more plausible that at least a lot of kinds of work are going to be automated out of existence in the foreseeable future. But I still think — and here again I agree with Gourevitch — that we’re always going to have some people working. Crucially, we’re always going to need people to make decisions and oversee the machines that are doing labor. I also think there are lots of kinds of work, especially care work or “ connective labor ,” that seem to essentially involve human-to-human interaction: whether that’s health care or childcare or therapy, or the kind of interactions that we take for granted at, say, a bar or a restaurant or a coffee shop. Now, under capitalism a lot of those workers are horribly exploited and not paid enough. But I don’t think an ideal socialist society would get rid of service work. I think those kinds of jobs can and should persist under socialism; workers should just be paid better and treated better and have more say over their working conditions. So even if AI and automation get rid of a lot of work, I think there will still always be work to do, and we need to have an idea of how we’re going to divvy that up and get people to do it. Can Moral Motivation Do the Job? Neal Meyer The second argument you take on is this idea that moral motivation can be a substitute: that people should be exhorted to work harder to do these jobs, and that in a socialist society, these kinds of moral appeals will be sufficient to get people to do the necessary work. What problems do you see here? Nick French A natural thought is that, if people have to work and we accept that there’s a duty to work, in a socialist society, we don’t want people to be motivated either by the threat of force or by “the dull compulsion of economic relations,” as Karl Marx put it — i.e., if you don’t work, you’ll starve. Instead, the idea is that we all come together, we democratically decide what work has to get done, and then, because we all see the value in contributing to the social project, we’ll all be motivated by the goodness of our hearts or our sense of duty to do what needs to be done. My view is this seems to imply a very big change in human motivation from what we see today, and that there’s an unrealistically altruistic or moralistic conception of human nature and human psychology at play. Again, to go back to the original argument for a duty to work: work is often something that we don’t want to do. It imposes significant burdens. In choosing to work, I’m often choosing to do something where, if I’m left to my own devices, I would rather do something else. The idea that you’re going to rely on these kinds of intrinsic moral motivations across a whole national or international economy, bringing together people who have no connection to each other, or maybe even have historical conflicts with one another — that you’re going to get them all to work out of a sense of duty — is just unrealistic. I’m not saying it’s impossible. But in setting forward a vision of socialism, we shouldn’t rely on assuming unrealistic changes in human psychology. We should present something that is feasible given human beings as we know and understand them. Coercion and Compulsion Neal Meyer Before we move on to your positive argument, I wanted to go back to the topic of coercion. You’re not saying that all attempts to get people to work are necessarily immoral or wrong or unjust. There are cases where some amount of compulsion may be necessary. Nick French I want to separate two issues here. The first goes into the positive case I make for labor markets. We can imagine a just society in which people are motivated in part by monetary gain. There’s not necessarily anything wrong with trying to realize compliance with a duty to work by having a basic income or some social minimum that everyone is guaranteed, but then saying, “Hey, if you want to make more than that, you do have to work.” Then you have different jobs that are paying people different amounts of money. But I’ll come back to that. The second issue is there might be certain jobs that, for various reasons, not enough people want to do, even if you pay them a lot of extra money — either because they require rare skills or talents, or because they involve a lot of drudgery, or because they’re especially hazardous. The classic example is sanitation workers. Maybe the robots will solve that one day; they don’t seem to be doing it yet. But until then, we’re still going to need people to collect and sort garbage. It’s drudgery, and it’s very hazardous work. We don’t want the market to assign that to whoever happens to want to take those jobs. I’m very sympathetic to recent proposals by folks like Lucas Stanczyk and Jan Kandiyali that people might be forced to take these jobs. I’m especially sympathetic to this idea when it comes to a kind of limited rotation. Maybe everyone should have a year or two of national civil service where they have to work as a sanitation worker, or they have to work cleaning hospitals, or something like that — work that involves more drudgery or is more hazardous. That’s a way of fairly sharing more extreme burdens of work. It’s also a way of inculcating a sense of civic duty and solidarity, that we’re all in this together. Where I would draw the line is when it gets to a point that you’re really interfering with freedom of choice of occupation, where you’re forcing people to work for long periods of time, where you’re no longer allowing them to autonomously set the direction of their lives and decide how they want to develop and exercise their creative capacities. There’s some room for a kind of coercive work regime in the kind of socialism I’m envisioning, but it has to be limited so that we are still respecting freedom of choice of occupation. Neal Meyer One of the interesting questions, when thinking about the difference between a socialist society and a capitalist society, is: What kinds of jobs do people need to be incentivized to take? Under capitalism, the assumption is people need to be incentivized to take jobs that require a lot of training, or a lot of autonomy and decision-making, or a lot of organizational skills or people skills. These are jobs that, in a socialist society where there was greater equality of opportunity, a lot of people would have the opportunity to get and would want to take. You can think of a whole list of occupations today that people get paid a lot of money to do that have their own intrinsic rewards besides the financial incentive. Under socialism, I would imagine those jobs are not going to pay as much, because a lot of people are going to be willing and able to do them. The jobs that are going to pay a lot are going to be the ones that require a lot of physical labor, that put you at risk, that are onerous or undesirable for many reasons. There’s going to be a kind of flipping of what needs to be incentivized in a transition from capitalism to socialism. Nick French That’s how I’m thinking about it. If you have an institutional framework in which firms are collectively owned, where people have equal opportunity in terms of access to high-quality education, and society is really trying to make jobs available to everyone, and also you do have a generous welfare-state social minimum, so that when people are unemployed it’s not an absolute personal disaster — they have that extra leverage. They can walk away from jobs; they’re not desperate to take the first offer that comes into view. We wouldn’t expect as many people to be forced by the market into the more difficult jobs. The Case for Labor Markets Neal Meyer We’ve cleared out some of the alternative ideas about how to handle the work problem in a better society. You come to the conclusion that labor markets have a really important role to play. Could you define what you mean by “labor markets,” and why you think they’re an important part of a vision for socialism? Nick French By a labor market, I mean that you have firms — whether they’re public sector firms or cooperatives that are owned or managed by their workers — where people can be attracted to those positions by the offer of a certain wage, and they take those jobs because they offer a certain wage. There can be pay differentials to attract people to jobs and firms where they’re most needed. This fits into a broader vision of market socialism . The core case for this is provided by the moral arguments we discussed, and also the case against the alternatives. Because there is a duty to work — people need to work, and they ought to do so, and we ought to share that burden equally — and because people’s freedom of choice of occupation should be respected, the best way of realizing both of those principles is a labor market. To clarify what I have in mind: Again, this is a socialist society. Obviously, we all have a lot of objections to the way labor markets work under capitalism, which we’ve already talked about. People are forced to take certain jobs because if they don’t, they’ll be on the street; they’ll starve. Also, when they take those jobs, they’re submitting to the tyranny of bosses who are not accountable to them in any way, who are following their own unconstrained profit imperatives. Again, I’m imagining a situation in which the relevant employers are democratically worker-managed firms, or public sector enterprises that are democratically accountable to the public, where workers have strong collective bargaining rights and protections. Once you have those things in place, and once you have a strong social minimum provided by a welfare state — decommodified health care, free, high-quality education, and something like a universal basic income, so even if you’re not working, you have money to spend on clothes, shoes, and so on — I don’t think there’s any objection per se to a labor market. Now, there are practical concerns that you might have about how this all works that I talk about in the paper. One of them is: If you have a really generous welfare state, or a generous basic income, what’s the incentive going to be for people to actually take jobs? We already said we’re not legally forcing people to take certain jobs. If that mute compulsion of economic relations isn’t there, is this really feasible? I point to the evidence from really existing, generous social democracies, in the Nordic countries for example, that seems to show that having more robust welfare states doesn’t negatively affect people’s participation in the labor force or economic growth. So we have good reason to be optimistic that having a very generous social minimum is compatible with a dynamic labor market. That said, I would acknowledge that if you make that social minimum too generous, then at some point you will lose that motivation that’s provided by offering people extra pay to take certain jobs. There’s always going to be some sort of balancing act. Probably, in our ideal socialist society, we’re going to have to do some trial and error to find where exactly that ideal social minimum lies. But I’m confident that we can ensure everyone a dignified existence. Neal Meyer People might ask, well, what about those people who can’t work, for whatever reason, or who retire? Presumably they would be offered a higher-than-minimum income. Nick French Yeah. Again, actually existing welfare states point in the direction of what a socialist society should do too, which is: if people have disabilities that prevent them from working, or if they’ve reached retirement age, they get an additional stipend above and beyond what they would get if they were working age and not judged to be disabled. That’s a fair way of managing things: to think that there’s some population we define as working age and capable that receives that basic dignified social minimum but also experiences an economic pressure to join the labor force. Neal Meyer One thing that might be worth also clarifying here is that, in your version of a labor market for socialism, we’re not talking about the kind of society we live in, where there’s no limit to the amount of income that someone can accumulate. The idea is to have a much more egalitarian wage structure. Nick French Definitely. My thought is that you want to allow inequalities insofar as that is necessary for providing everyone the means to flourish. I’m not coming down hard on an exact view about what the most just income distribution looks like. But I do think something like John Rawls’s difference principle is really compelling: you allow for inequalities in wealth and income insofar as those benefit the worst off. Now, the kinds of inequalities that would exist because of pay differentials to get people to take certain jobs are going to be way smaller than exist under capitalism. There are a few reasons for that. One is that I do think people will be more intrinsically motivated in a society that is more solidaristic and where there’s more equality of opportunity. And when more of the economy is under public ownership and less driven by the profit motive, when you have collective bargaining regimes in place that guarantee workers certain minimums and sectoral benchmarks, as we’ve seen in places like Sweden, you’re not going to see runaway pay for executives. We’ve gotten rid of the capitalist class, so you don’t have capitalists hoarding wealth as individuals. So, there’s still inequality, but way less. articles.title: The Rising Congressional Left Is Positioned Well
articles.author: Branko Marcetic
articles.content: In a bitter disappointment for the Left, Hakeem Jeffries — the vehemently pro-Israel Wall Street darling who once , bizarrely, did a version of George Wallace’s infamous “segregation forever” speech, only subbing in “Israel” for “segregation” — will be the next speaker of the House of Representatives. The vote wasn’t even close: 251–11, with two members abstaining, something Jeffries’s allies are already celebrating as a sign of his domination of the Democratic caucus. Going into this election, the members of the expanded Squad — the twenty or so progressives and socialists elected to Congress who may or may not now be known as “The Bloc” — viewed the two years between now and 2028 as a vital, possibly final, chance for Democrats to deliver some actual results for working people and avert future political disaster. Jeffries’s ascension to the speaker’s gavel drastically reduces the chances of that happening. That’s the pessimistic way to look at it, at least. There is also a rosier perspective. But to start with, there’s a lot to be pessimistic about. Hakeem Jeffries is a champion of political and economic elites. He and the rest of the House leadership are largely funded by the exact industries — finance, defense, health insurers and pharmaceuticals, the crypto industry, and firms like Palantir — that are militantly against the kind of change that people voted his party into power to see. His ambitious agenda if Democrats won was to reverse a handful of policies Donald Trump had enacted last year, including ending the Iran war, and simply bring us back to the intolerable status quo ante that produced Trump’s election in the first place. Jeffries is already punting on the budding plan to end the war by defunding it. He has refused to commit to even holding a vote on US aid to Israel, putting him at odds with not just a large supermajority of his party’s own voters but most of the American public. Jeffries is, in other words, an embodiment of everything people do not like about the Democratic Party, which is more or less what incoming Ohio Rep. Don Leonard told him in a closed-door meeting, a sentiment Jeffries apparently gets. Upon telling the speaker-to-be to his face that his name was “synonymous” with the “low quality” of today’s Democratic Party brand, Jeffries, according to Leonard, nodded. Socialists and progressives did not even try to mount a challenge to Jeffries, seemingly confirming fears that the blowout margin of the Democrats’ midterm win would, paradoxically, produce a more conservative outcome by shrinking the Left’s leverage. The party’s left-populist wing made the calculation that Jeffries simply had unassailable numbers, thanks in no small part to his lockstep support from the powerful Congressional Black Caucus (CBC), which views the history-making aspect of the first black House speaker as critically important, regardless of that speaker’s actual politics. Some progressives have also pointed to the lack of viable (or really, any) challenger to Jeffries to explain the failure to move against him, which is partially true. They still could have tried to muster enough members to oppose him that it would make his eventual path to the speakership (for which the actual, full House vote will take place next year) more difficult and eventually wring concessions out of him, as the GOP’s Freedom Caucus did to Kevin McCarthy three years ago. The counterargument to this is that Republicans in 2023 had a far slimmer majority than the Democrats will have — just nine seats, compared to the Democrats’ eighty-five seats and counting next year — and that they did this on the back of a GOP midterm performance widely viewed as a flop compared to the Democrats’ historic overperformance this year, which Jeffries’s allies like the CBC wasted no time in crediting him personally with. In any case, the party’s left bloc — which, of course, is still getting its bearings and hasn’t even been sworn in yet in Congress — decided the slim chances of rolling Jeffries wasn’t worth the risk of drawing his ire. The strongest, “steel man” argument for this is that they have done something similar to Zohran Mamdani in New York, who likewise calculated that, given his relatively weak position as a newly elected insurgent mayor, there was no plausible pathway to challenging centrist Democrats in New York, and he would be more successful if he avoided spending political capital on what he viewed as a suicide mission. That decision saw Mamdani effectively quash a Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) primary endorsement against Jeffries last year, both to keep the powerful Democratic leader out of his hair as he got his nascent mayoralty going and because he assessed that such a challenge could not win, and ally himself with centrist governor Kathy Hochul, betting he could accomplish the kinds of legislative victories he needed to succeed as mayor by cozying up to the governor (who holds significantly more power across multiple fronts) than by antagonizing her. Both of those proved to be successful bets for Mamdani. We’ve gotten some idea of what the consequences for crossing Jeffries could look like from Leonard, who last week revealed party leadership had threatened to make him lose reelection in two years time if he didn’t get behind the Brooklyn Democrat. Other than Leonard, from what we know so far, the others who voted against Jeffries were almost all socialist freshmen in safe blue districts — or, in the case of incoming Reps. Frederick Haynes III and Adam Hamawy, Medicare for All–supporting progressives in safe blue districts. In other words, the votes against Jeffries are from members who have nothing to lose and in fact could benefit politically in the long run from going on the record opposing someone expected to be a disappointing speaker. By one view, this failure to block Jeffries will be fatal to the party and to any hope of it pursuing a pro-working-class agenda. Shortly after the result, Corbin Trent, cofounder of Justice Democrats and former staffer to both the Bernie Sanders presidential campaigns and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, had told me his fears that the Democrats would fail “if the same people who drove this bus of the party into the hands of Donald Trump twice” stayed in place, meaning Jeffries and his Senate counterpart, Chuck Schumer. Trent has spread that message elsewhere , including on Fox News , where he appeared to not-so-subtly prod his former boss, Ocasio-Cortez, to be more outspoken in this fight, saying that anyone planning to run for president in 2028 “should be voicing up now.” As a number of incumbent and incoming left-insurgent lawmakers told me in the process of reporting a forthcoming In These Times piece on the midterm result, a Democratic failure to deliver results, or even to appear to be trying to deliver them, could spark another Obama era–like mass disillusionment that could end up empowering someone much worse than Trump not far down the line. According to the pessimistic view of where things currently stand, we are well on the way to that future right now. But again, that’s not the only way to assess what happened here. Jeffries Isn’t Out of the Woods There is good reason not to swallow wholesale the corporate center’s triumphalism over the vote margin, which the corruption-tainted Rep. Henry Cuellar gloated showed the opposition to Jeffries is just “a small number of votes that are marginalized” and that “this small little group cannot tell the caucus where we need to be at.” Those reasons go beyond the fact that some version of this line is what this crowd has constantly been telling themselves as their grip on the party has slowly faded the past ten years. In advance of the vote, Jeffries had already moved on his initial, tepid program of Trump reversals by publicly endorsing Bernie Sanders’s Medicare expansion plan over the weekend. Sanders’s proposal — lowering the Medicare eligibility age to fifty-five, including dental, vision, and hearing in the program, and covering all children with it until they turn nineteen — was not something any Democrat brought up or ran on during the midterms. Yet Jeffries’s adoption of it means it’s quickly becoming a consensus position among both the Democrats’ populist and corporate wings since the Vermont senator first brought it up two days after the election. This would not be a minor reform. It would extend free public health insurance to 3.45 million adults and anywhere from four–seven million kids, depending on exactly how many children are thrown off health insurance in the years ahead by Trump’s Medicaid cuts. It would go much further than the Medicare-related parts of Joe Biden’s popular but never-passed Build Back Better bill, which merely added hearing to the program’s coverage, and would go a long way toward alleviating voters’ cost-of-living concerns, since health care is one of the biggest, most stress-inducing, and sometimes life-ruining costs anyone can deal with in today’s United States. Left-insurgent lawmakers view the next two years as a unique opportunity: either they pass something that Trump actually ends up signing into law, making good on their election promises and tangibly making voters’ lives better, or Trump vetoes a bunch of things they pass, letting them make the argument to voters in 2028 that they need a Democratic president in the White House. If Jeffries’s movement on this matter holds, it will put socialists and progressives in a decent position to actually pursue this strategy. Meanwhile, the fact that Jeffries has moved suggests he’s more vulnerable than the numbers today make it seem. Jeffries has, incredibly, a worse approval rating than outgoing Republican House speaker Mike Johnson, and while he at least gets overall positive marks from Kamala Harris voters, liberals, and Democrats — three of the paltry four groups he’s not underwater with — he gets them just barely, unable to muster majority support from any of those three. More worrying for Jeffries, his congressional district, New York’s 8th, where he will have to contest a primary election in just two years’ time, is deep in DSA territory , in a state and city where the socialist organization has emerged over the past year as a leading political power . To its immediate north is the 7th district, where DSA member and Mamdani ally Claire Valdez (who just voted against Jeffries) easily bested the Brooklyn borough president for the seat, and at whose watch party DSA members chanted “You’re next!” when Jeffries came on the screen. Bordering its panhandle to the west is the heavily Jewish 10th district, where another Mamdani ally, Brad Lander, comfortably ousted one of the Democrats’ most well-financed and most ardently pro-Israel members of Congress by taking direct aim at his unconditional support for Israel’s genocide. A little further up, and you get to the kingdom of another Mamdani ally and DSA member, Ocasio-Cortez, who eight years ago made her 14th district the final resting place for the career of a different corporate Democrat once tipped to be a future speaker. In other words, for the sake of his career, Jeffries has to watch his left flank for the next couple years. A misstep, or a series of them, where he ends up looking like the singular roadblock to Democrats’ progressive ambitions, will be a weakness that a future primary challenger will eagerly exploit. Piling on the pressure is the fact that next year’s Democrat-led Senate is now looking like a far more progressive chamber than usual. Besides Sanders, the country’s most prominent and well-liked socialist, it will feature three of his endorsees (Abdul El-Sayed, Troy Jackson, and Peggy Flanagan), all of whom campaigned on Medicare for All, and sixteen others who — however disingenuously — endorsed Sanders’s legislation on the program last year, as well as one other — Ron Wyden — who has come around to the idea in the past year, and vowed to use his coming chairmanship of the Senate Finance Committee to push through an expansion of the program. It’s notable that the bold idea to risk a government shutdown in order to force Trump to end the Iran war originated from the Senate, and so far has the sign-on of not just Sanders and Chris Van Hollen — who has spent the past twenty-two months courting progressive support for a potential 2028 run — but centrists Michael Bennet and Tammy Duckworth. It’s notable, too, that Jeffries felt he had to go along with the Medicare expansion proposal, another progressive idea that came out of the Senate. What happens in the Senate majority leadership race could intensify this dynamic. If Schumer — who is more vulnerable than Jeffries and underwater with the left-leaning demographics that still give the future speaker a slim positive approval rating — really is replaced by the more progressive Van Hollen, it may add further pressure on Jeffries, given that he can’t politically afford to look like he’s stymieing the party’s agenda or undermining its resistance to Trump. None of this is guaranteed, and it’s possible in a few months to a year, this will all read as wildly overoptimistic. But the opposite, pessimistic case isn’t guaranteed either, and there are reasons to think that the Democrats’ populist wing of socialists and progressives has cards it’s yet to play, as it once more thanklessly drags the party into saving itself. Jeffries’s victory yesterday is certainly a blow for the Left. But it’s not out of the question that in hindsight, it looks more like losing a battle while winning the war. articles.content: We talk about "kitchen table politics" as if it were a place free of culture, a neutral ground of gas prices and grocery bills where the culture wars are an unwelcome distraction. Anyone who has actually sat at one knows better. The kitchen table is where the culture war is fought, and it is fought by people who love you. articles.title: Slow-Motion Atomic Bomb
articles.author: Tom Engelhardt
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. In some sense, all of us on this planet of... well, I was going to say ours, but I’m not so sure anymore... are living through a slow-motion cataclysm, a first-class global apocalypse in the making. As a headline on the World Meteorological Organization’s website put it recently , “State of the climate in 2026 gives new meaning to phrase ‘off the charts.’” Here in the United States in the age of Donald Trump, though, you’d hardly know it. You might even say that, in some sense, the subject is MIA or missing in action. Count on this: If even one atomic bomb were ever to be used in a war in this world of ours, it would be the headline story across this country and planet. And yet, though seldom thought of that way, climate change is essentially the equivalent of a slow-motion atomic attack on this very planet of ours. However, in the age of Donald Trump, who grabs the headlines day after endless day, it goes remarkably unnoticed. Related: Trump, Climate Change, and the Decline of the American Empire It seems to matter little that the weather is already setting new heat records regularly or, as U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said all too vividly recently: “We have entered a new age of climate extremes. A supersized El Niño is colliding with a planet already superheated by manmade climate change. Climate records keep falling. The human costs keep rising. And those least responsible are suffering first and worst.” Whether you think about it or not, believe me, it’s happening and, barring surprising action, it’s going to be a first-class nightmare for our children and grandchildren. Imagine this: the other day, November 7th to be exact, for the first time this fall I added a sweater to my very light jacket and shirt on my morning walk here in New York City and also switched from khakis to blue jeans. (The very next day, however, that sweater was gone and I was back in those khakis.) As it happens, I have yet to put on my fall leather jacket, which, once upon a time, I would normally have started wearing daily by at least mid-October (if not before). Buy the Book Not in 2026, though, not on this already distinctly overheating planet of ours. Or as the World Meteorological Society reminds us , “The past 12 years have individually been the warmest on record, with the past four years being the top four. The global average surface temperature for January–September 2026 was about 1.47 °Celsius above the pre-industrial average. This figure is likely to rise through the end of the year because of the warming effect of El Niño, which has been intensifying since August and is expected to be the strongest on record by December.” Whew! I’m already sweating! In fact, while I was writing this piece, the United Nations Climate Change Conference’s annual summit, known as COP31, was underway in Turkey with 197 countries attending. However, my country and “my” president—shock! shock!—didn’t send a delegation. (Some congressional Democrats did attend , but without the usual State Department assistance!). And if you didn’t even notice, I’m not faintly surprised. After all, it was covered in the media here in an exceedingly modest fashion. This old guy, for instance, still subscribes to and reads (on paper, believe it or not!) the New York Times and it did cover the start of that conference. Its article on the subject , however, was relegated to page 10 of the paper on a day when (of course!) the major front-page headline article was about YKEW (You Know Exactly Whom): “Clear Message to Trump, But Hazy Future for U.S., Parties Face a Gap Until His Term Ends.” And the theme of that article was all too apt after the Republican midterm election losses: “Mr. Trump may be wounded, but a wounded animal can thrash around powerfully.” After a fashion, the climate did manage to sneak onto that paper’s front page in an area at the bottom right headlined , “War Both Slows and Advances Quest for an Energy Transition.” (Note, by the way, that both headlines were different in the online version of the paper.) Related: Welcome to Trumpworld, Where Political Reality Defies Belief Unfortunately, one way “our” president does indeed continue to thrash around is exactly in terms of the climate, and that story, as I mentioned, was relegated to page 10. Think, in fact, of climate change as essentially missing in action in our all-American news world. And yet, although seldom thought of that way, it should essentially be considered the slow-motion equivalent of an atomic attack on this planet. Unfortunately, in the age of Donald Trump, who all too literally grabs the headlines, day after endless day, who among us would be interested in anything happening in such relatively slow motion? Certainly not our president who, only recently in a typical ramble , began on the subject of transgender athletes, then wandered to George Washington’s possible thoughts on the subject. (”George Washington lived in sanity. He didn’t have men playing in women’s sports. I promise you this. I didn’t know George Washington personally, but they did not have the mutilization of your children for transgender purposes.”) Next, he moved on to how a young man from Israel had asked him who his favorite president was, leading him to Abraham Lincoln and only then concluding—if that’s faintly the word for it with him!—this way: “‘Oh.’ I said, ‘That’s nice.’ We love Abraham Lincoln. But you’re going to see something later, because they have a poll—they took a poll recently. You’re going to see it. But I also declared a national emergency on energy and terminated the Green New Scam, one of the greatest hoaxes in the history of our country.” Ah, it’s all clear now, right? Our Scamster-in-Chief, a modern Abraham Lincoln, is intent on wiping the Green New Scam from our very attention span. And why not when, having just gotten clobbered in the midterm elections, he promptly appointed Stephen Miller to be his new White House chief of staff? We’re talking, of course, about the major architect of the president’s mass deportation policy, not to speak of his “hardline crackdown on immigration”—you know, the very policy that Trump himself recently admitted “might have been too tough” in election season. A Hell on Earth? And as passingly strange as all of that might be, it’s my personal reminder that this 82-year-old is, day by day, on a distinctly different planet from anything he once knew or imagined. Generally, if you were paying attention to the mainstream news, though, you would hardly know it. For instance, every night I watch the NBC evening news and then the PBS News, and NBC absolutely loves reporting on climate disasters—floods, tornadoes, raging wildfires, you name it, almost any night of the week. But when it comes to truly naming things, endless weeks can pass without anyone on that news crew even mentioning climate change in passing. Now, as I said, I also watch the PBS evening news and when they report on the growing climate disasters in this country and world of ours, they do tend to mention climate change. But it’s seldom the equivalent of headline material. Nor is it, of course, in the paper New York Times , which I still read daily, and which certainly repor ts on the subject, but not faintly the way it reports, of course(!), on that Washington climate disaster, Donald J. Trump. The one mainstream publication I read that, on a daily basis, deals with climate change in a fashion that seems genuinely appropriate is the British paper, the Guardian , which, believe it or not, actually has an online “climate crisis” section featuring new articles just about every day on the subject. As I was writing this very paragraph, in fact, it typically had these three headlines: “ Slight fall in carbon emissions from fossil fuels as Iran war drives renewables push “; “ Tuesday briefing: The world is falling short on climate action. Can Cop31 change that? “; “ High fossil fuel prices spread inflation ‘like a cancer,’ UN climate chief tells Cop31 .” Related: Climate Change Is a Slow-Motion Nuclear War—and We're Already Counting the Dead And it even writes up its reports on the climate in a striking fashion. Here’s just a typical sentence from a piece I also read as I was writing this: “The world is heading for an ‘irrecoverable overshoot’ of global temperature thresholds that will plunge billions of people into disastrous climate impacts because governments have stalled for so long to cut planet-heating emissions, analysis has found.” And yes, we’re in a world where such coverage should make all too much sense to all of us. But normally, when you’re not being hit by the latest heat wave, tornado, or weather disaster of whatever sort, you simply wouldn’t know from most of the media that we’re in a potentially world-destroying situation (at least as we’ve known it all these centuries), just in (relatively) slow motion. Nor, if you live in the United States, would you normally have the faintest idea that, as the Guardian reported recently , “while all the other 20 major economies reduced or slowed their carbon pollution last year, the U.S. was a ‘major exception’ by emitting an extra 133m tons of planet-heating gases from the burning of coal, oil and gas.” Nor, for that matter, would you be likely to know that “heat is accumulating in Earth’s systems at an accelerating rate, the UN’s weather agency has reported as the Cop31 climate change summit begins in Turkey, with 2026 on track to be one of the four warmest years on record.” Phew! I’m already sweating! So here we are, distinctly in a new age of ever-increasing climate extremes, with a climate-crazed president in the White House and other climate ignorers like Russia’s Vladimir Putin right before our global eyes. Yet, if you’re not listening to someone like U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres, you essentially might never truly know it (or at least take it in). And the more we wait to face our present reality, while allowing figures like Trump and Putin to control major countries on this planet, the less likely it is that we’ll be able to deal with that onrushing global future and save ourselves from—all too literally—a hell on Earth.
