articles.title: Las elecciones masivas de China y la política más allá de las urnas
articles.author: Tings Chak
articles.content: Read in English here En toda China se está llevando a cabo uno de los procesos de votación directa más grandes del mundo. A lo largo de los años 2026 y 2027, se convoca a más de mil millones de votantes elegibles para elegir a más de 2,6 millones de diputados para los congresos populares de condados y municipios. Desde la capital, Pekín, hasta las vastas zonas rurales, las elecciones se llevan a cabo a una escala que rara vez se ve en otros lugares; sin embargo, esta faceta del sistema político chino sigue siendo poco conocida en el extranjero. A finales de septiembre, en la aldea de Li’an, cerca de Wuxi, en la provincia de Jiangsu, al este de China, los preparativos para las elecciones adoptaron una forma inusual . Durante un festival de música rural en la granja Yushan, los representantes electos sirvieron café recién molido a los agricultores locales y a los visitantes. Entre ellos se encontraba Lu Jinlian, diputada del Congreso Popular del municipio, quien se sentó con los residentes en lo que los organizadores denominaron un “ salón de campo ” (田间会客厅), para hablar sobre el desarrollo de la aldea y alentar a las personas a registrarse y prepararse para votar. El café no se sirvió en un centro de votación, ni se trató simplemente de un gesto propio de la época electoral. La granja, que antes estaba en desuso, ahora reúne actividades agrícolas, presentaciones musicales y la vida comunitaria del pueblo. Su transformación también ha acercado a los residentes y a sus representantes electos para abordar inquietudes prácticas, como el acceso a la granja y los caminos sin iluminación entre los campos. Según informes locales, los diputados dieron seguimiento a estas solicitudes y ayudaron a lograr mejoras. Dichos intercambios forman parte del trabajo habitual de la estación de enlace representativa de Li’an, que organiza estas actividades mensuales, llevando los debates fuera de su oficina y hacia los huertos, las granjas y los campos, entre la gente. En Pekín, el mismo proceso electoral se desarrolló a escala metropolitana. El 6 de noviembre, la capital estableció 13.054 centros de votación para elegir a 4898 diputados de distrito y 11.137 diputados de municipio. La votación se llevó a cabo en comunidades residenciales, lugares de trabajo, campus universitarios e instituciones estatales, incluido Zhongnanhai, donde el presidente Xi Jinping emitió su voto. Luo Ling, una residente centenaria del distrito de Dongcheng, votó desde su silla de ruedas. En la sede de Tencent en Pekín, los repartidores de comida se unieron a los empleados de la empresa en un centro de votación ubicado dentro del edificio de oficinas. Este sistema se extiende por todo un país con 503.000 aldeas administrativas y 112.000 comunidades urbanas . A finales de 2020, los diputados de condado y de municipio constituían el 94,5% de los 2,62 millones de representantes que desempeñaban sus funciones en los cinco niveles de los congresos populares. Los comités de aldea tienen sus propias elecciones y responsabilidades, distintas de las de los congresos populares. Sin embargo, la importancia de la representación va más allá de transmitir las inquietudes locales a los funcionarios del Gobierno. Los congresos populares supervisan la labor del Gobierno, revisan los presupuestos y los planes de desarrollo, y eligen y supervisan a los funcionarios locales. En principio, servir al pueblo significa no solo responder a las necesidades inmediatas, sino también representar sus intereses en las decisiones sobre la dirección del desarrollo económico y social. Establecido formalmente en septiembre de 1954, cinco años después de la fundación de la República Popular de China, el sistema de congresos populares opera actualmente en cinco niveles, en los que los ciudadanos eligen directamente a los diputados para los congresos de condado o de distrito urbano y para los congresos de municipio, cada uno con un mandato de cinco años. Los congresos de las ciudades, las provincias y la Asamblea Popular Nacional (APN) son elegidos indirectamente por los congresos del nivel inferior. Este proceso dará lugar a una nueva legislatura nacional en 2028. Mientras tanto, el Partido Comunista de China (PCC) también se está preparando para su 21.º Congreso Nacional en 2027 , mediante un proceso electoral independiente dentro del Partido. En conjunto, estas instituciones forman parte de la organización política del Estado socialista de China, aunque el Partido y los sistemas de congresos populares tienen funciones distintas pero complementarias. De conformidad con la ley electoral de China , los ciudadanos mayores de dieciocho años pueden votar y postularse a las elecciones. El PCC y los otros ocho partidos políticos de China, que operan dentro del sistema político bajo el liderazgo del PCC, pueden presentar candidatos a los congresos populares, al igual que las organizaciones de masas y los grupos de diez o más votantes que actúen de manera conjunta. Algunas de las normas que rigen este sistema electoral incluyen el requisito de que participe más de la mitad de los votantes registrados, que un candidato obtenga más de la mitad de los votos, que haya más candidatos que escaños y que la votación sea secreta. Es a través de estas disposiciones que se establece un proceso mediante el cual los residentes pueden nominar y elegir a quienes los representarán en las instituciones locales, en lugar de que los representantes sean simplemente designados desde arriba. En Pekín, la oficina electoral municipal informó que la gran mayoría de los candidatos fueron propuestos por grupos de diez o más votantes – el 85% de los 7,337 candidatos a nivel de distrito y el 90.8% de los 16,683 candidatos a nivel de municipio –, mientras que el resto fue recomendado por partidos políticos y organizaciones de masas. Las mujeres representaron el 46.3% y el 48.5% de las listas de candidatos respectivas. Antes de la votación, grupos de votantes discutieron a los candidatos preliminares, tras lo cual los comités electorales determinaron y publicaron las listas definitivas. También se organizaron reuniones para que los candidatos se presentaran y respondieran a las inquietudes de los votantes. En el distrito de Shijingshan, cuatro candidatos se reunieron con residentes que les preguntaron sobre los servicios para personas mayores, la administración de propiedades y las actividades deportivas infantiles. Este proceso de nominación, consulta y selección revela un aspecto de la participación popular que es exclusivo del sistema político de China y poco conocido fuera del país. En Li’an, las conversaciones entre los diputados y los residentes comenzaron mucho antes de la temporada de votaciones. Lu Jinlian también administra un café rural , donde ella y el diputado Qiang Tianyu reunieron a representantes de la aldea, agricultores y jóvenes que habían regresado a su pueblo natal para iniciar negocios. Entre 2012 y 2025, más de 13 millones de personas en toda China regresaron o se mudaron a zonas rurales para iniciar negocios, incluyendo un número cada vez mayor de jóvenes graduados y profesionales. En junio, los participantes discutieron cómo vincular la agricultura con el turismo y crear nuevos medios de sustento en el campo. Entre las cinco propuestas que surgieron de estos debates se encontraba una ruta ciclista que conectara huertos locales, casas de huéspedes y atracciones turísticas, con iluminación para alentar a los visitantes a quedarse más tiempo. Se trataba de propuestas, no de proyectos terminados, pero muestran las inquietudes que los residentes planteaban a sus representantes y formaron parte de un mes de actividades de los congresos populares en todo el municipio de Yangjian, en las que participaron más de 500 personas en docenas de eventos destinados a recabar sugerencias del público. A través de su participación en los congresos populares, los diputados cuentan con canales para incorporar estas inquietudes a los debates sobre planes de desarrollo, gasto público y la labor del Gobierno, vinculando las preocupaciones cotidianas de los aldeanos con decisiones más amplias sobre el futuro del campo. Cuando llegó el festival en septiembre, los diputados aprovecharon esas relaciones para fomentar la participación electoral. Durante el registro de votantes de octubre , el municipio de Yangjian dividió su territorio en distritos electorales, publicó avisos, realizó visitas a los hogares y se puso en contacto con los residentes que trabajaban lejos de casa, a menudo en otras ciudades – un tema fundamental en un país donde la migración laboral ha transformado la relación entre el campo y los centros urbanos. Para llegar a las personas que fácilmente podrían pasar por alto un aviso en el tablón de anuncios de la aldea se requiere movilización y creatividad, desde llamadas telefónicas y visitas a los hogares hasta debates públicos alrededor de una mesa de café en el festival local. El derecho a la representación ha cambiado en sí mismo durante la construcción socialista de China. Según la ley electoral de 1953, cada diputado rural al Congreso Nacional representaba a ocho veces más personas que un diputado urbano. Si bien la proporción disminuyó en las décadas siguientes, fue en 2010 cuando se modificó la ley para asignar escaños sobre la misma base de población tanto en las zonas urbanas como en las rurales. La reforma no eliminó las desigualdades entre el campo y las ciudades, pero marcó un paso importante en los esfuerzos continuos del país por superar la brecha histórica, un desafío central de la construcción socialista. El Gobierno chino entiende que las elecciones, la consulta, la toma de decisiones y la supervisión forman parte de la “ democracia popular en todo el proceso ”. El liderazgo del Partido Comunista de China (PCC) está establecido en la Constitución, mientras que las elecciones a los congresos populares eligen a los representantes para los órganos del poder estatal, en lugar de determinar qué partido gobierna el país. Se espera que, a través de los congresos populares, los diputados incorporen las inquietudes de sus electores en las decisiones sobre los recursos públicos y el desarrollo, y que supervisen la labor del Gobierno. Si bien las experiencias desde la aldea de Li’an hasta la capital, Pekín, ofrecen una visión de estos procesos, no nos permiten saber cómo se resuelven todas las demandas en conflicto ni qué propuestas reciben financiamiento en última instancia. En toda China, más de mil millones de votantes con derecho a voto participan en elecciones que determinarán quién los representará en estas instituciones durante los próximos cinco años. En Li’an, los habitantes del pueblo están discutiendo cómo se puede desarrollar la producción agrícola, cómo los jóvenes pueden ganarse la vida en el campo y cómo la inversión pública puede mejorar su comunidad. Estas son preguntas que van mucho más allá de un solo pueblo. Forman parte del esfuerzo continuo de China por transformar la relación entre el pueblo y las instituciones del poder estatal, y por determinar quién participa en la configuración del futuro del país. Tings Chak (翟庭君) es la coordinadora adjunta para Asia de Tricontinental: Instituto de Investigación Social y editora de Wenhua Zongheng: Revista de pensamiento chino contemporáneo . articles.title: China’s massive elections and politics beyond the ballot box
articles.author: Tings Chak
articles.content: Lee en español aquí Across China, one of the world’s largest direct voting processes is underway. Throughout 2026 and 2027, more than one billion eligible voters are being called upon to elect over 2.6 million delegates to county and municipal people’s congresses. From the capital, Beijing, to the vast rural areas, the elections are being held on a scale rarely seen elsewhere; yet this facet of the Chinese political system remains little known abroad. In late September, in Li’an Village near Wuxi, Jiangsu Province, eastern China, election preparations took an unusual form . During a rural music festival at Yushan Farm, elected officials served freshly ground coffee to local farmers and visitors. Among them was Lu Jinlian, a deputy to the municipal People’s Congress, who sat with residents in what organizers called a “ countryside lounge ” to discuss village development and encourage people to register and prepare to vote. The coffee wasn’t served at a polling station, nor was it simply an election-season gesture. The once-abandoned farm now hosts agricultural activities, musical performances, and community life. Its transformation has also brought residents and their elected representatives closer together to address practical concerns, such as farm access and unlit paths between fields. According to local reports, the representatives followed up on these requests and helped bring about improvements. Such exchanges are part of the regular work of the Li’an Representative Liaison Station, which organizes these monthly activities, taking discussions out of its office and into the orchards, farms, and fields – among the people. In Beijing, the same electoral process unfolded on a metropolitan scale. On November 6, the capital set up 13,054 polling stations to elect 4,898 district deputies and 11,137 borough deputies. Voting took place in residential communities, workplaces, university campuses, and state institutions, including Zhongnanhai, where President Xi Jinping cast his ballot. Luo Ling, a centenarian resident of Dongcheng District, voted from her wheelchair. At Tencent’s Beijing headquarters, food delivery drivers joined company employees at a polling station located inside the office building. This system spans a country with 503,000 administrative villages and 112,000 urban communities . At the end of 2020, county and municipal deputies comprised 94.5% of the 2.62 million representatives serving at the five levels of the people’s congresses. Village committees have their own elections and responsibilities, distinct from those of the people’s congresses. However, the importance of representation extends beyond simply conveying local concerns to government officials. The people’s congresses oversee the work of the government, review budgets and development plans, and elect and supervise local officials. In principle, serving the people means not only responding to immediate needs but also representing their interests in decisions about the direction of economic and social development. Formally established in September 1954, five years after the founding of the People’s Republic of China, the people’s congress system currently operates at five levels. Citizens directly elect deputies to county or urban district congresses and to municipal congresses, each serving a five-year term. City and provincial congresses, as well as the National People’s Congress (NPC), are indirectly elected by the lower-level congresses. This process will result in a new national legislature in 2028. Meanwhile, the Communist Party of China (CPC) is also preparing for its 21st National Congress in 2027 through a separate electoral process within the Party. Together, these institutions form part of the political organization of China’s socialist state, although the Party and the people’s congress systems have distinct but complementary functions. In accordance with China’s electoral law , citizens aged eighteen and over are eligible to vote and run for office. The Communist Party of China (CPC) and the eight other political parties operating within the CPC’s political system can nominate candidates for the People’s Congresses, as can mass organizations and groups of ten or more voters acting jointly. Some of the rules governing this electoral system include the requirement that more than half of registered voters participate, that a candidate receive more than half of the votes, that there be more candidates than seats, and that the ballot be secret. It is through these provisions that a process is established whereby residents can nominate and elect their representatives to local institutions, rather than representatives simply being appointed from above. In Beijing, the municipal election office reported that the vast majority of candidates were nominated by groups of ten or more voters – 85% of the 7,337 district-level candidates and 90.8% of the 16,683 borough-level candidates – while the remainder were recommended by political parties and mass organizations. Women comprised 46.3% and 48.5% of the respective candidate lists. Before the vote, groups of voters discussed the preliminary candidates, after which the election committees determined and published the final lists. Meetings were also organized for candidates to introduce themselves and answer voters’ questions. In Shijingshan District, four candidates met with residents who asked them about services for the elderly, property management, and children’s sports activities. This nomination, consultation, and selection process reveals an aspect of popular participation that is unique to China’s political system and little known outside the country. In Li’an, talks between lawmakers and residents began long before the election season. Lu Jinlian also runs a rural café , where she and lawmaker Qiang Tianyu brought together village representatives, farmers, and young people who had returned to their hometowns to start businesses. Between 2012 and 2025, more than 13 million people across China returned to or moved to rural areas to start businesses, including a growing number of young graduates and professionals. In June, participants discussed how to link agriculture with tourism and create new livelihoods in rural areas. Among the five proposals that emerged from these discussions was a cycling route connecting local orchards, guesthouses, and tourist attractions, with lighting to encourage visitors to stay longer. These were proposals, not finished projects, but they reflect the concerns residents were raising with their representatives and were part of a month-long series of people’s congresses across Yangjian Township, which involved more than 500 people in dozens of events designed to gather public input. Through their participation in the people’s congresses, delegates have channels to incorporate these concerns into discussions about development plans, government spending, and the work of the government, linking villagers’ everyday worries to broader decisions about the future of rural areas. When the festival arrived in September, lawmakers leveraged these relationships to encourage voter turnout. During voter registration in October , Yangjian Township divided its territory into electoral districts, posted notices, conducted door-to-door visits, and reached out to residents who worked far from home, often in other cities – a critical issue in a country where labor migration has transformed the relationship between rural and urban centers. Reaching people who might easily miss a notice on the village bulletin board requires mobilization and creativity, from phone calls and home visits to public discussions around a coffee table at the local festival. The right to representation has itself changed during China’s socialist construction. Under the 1953 election law, each rural deputy to the National Congress represented eight times more people than an urban deputy. While this ratio decreased in subsequent decades, it was in 2010 that the law was amended to allocate seats on the same population basis in both urban and rural areas. The reform did not eliminate inequalities between rural and urban areas, but it marked an important step in the country’s ongoing efforts to overcome the historical gap, a central challenge of socialist construction. The Chinese government understands that elections, consultation, decision-making, and oversight are all part of “ people’s democracy throughout the entire process .” The leadership of the Communist Party of China (CPC) is enshrined in the Constitution, while elections to people’s congresses choose representatives for organs of state power, rather than determining which party governs the country. Deputies are expected, through the people’s congresses, to incorporate the concerns of their constituents into decisions about public resources and development, and to oversee the work of the government. While experiences from Li’an village to the capital, Beijing, offer a glimpse into these processes, they do not reveal how all conflicting demands are resolved or which proposals ultimately receive funding. Across China, more than a billion eligible voters are participating in elections that will determine who will represent them in these institutions for the next five years. In Li’an, villagers are discussing how to develop agricultural production, how young people can earn a living in the countryside, and how public investment can improve their community. These are questions that extend far beyond a single village. They are part of China’s ongoing effort to transform the relationship between the people and the institutions of state power, and to determine who participates in shaping the country’s future. Tings Chak (翟庭君) is the deputy coordinator for Asia of Tricontinental: Institute for Social Research and editor of Wenhua Zongheng: Journal of Contemporary Chinese Thought . articles.title: Trump threatens to raise tariffs if Mexico does not stop a new migrant caravan
articles.author: Pablo Meriguet
articles.content: A new caravan of Latin American migrants heading north through Central America has brought to the fore the Trump administration’s anti-immigration policies and its pressure campaign on Mexico to stop the thousands of participants before they reach its borders. The administration of Republican Donald Trump reported that it is following the news closely with concern. In this regard, the US president threatened Mexico with doubling tariffs if it does not stop the caravan: “Here we go again! With the perceived loss by the Republicans in the midterms … the INVASION of our country is taking place again … They will not be accepted! MEXICO MUST STOP THEM, NOW, and if they do not do so, the tariffs on Mexico will be IMMEDIATELY DOUBLED,” Trump said in response to the possibility of the arrival of nearly 1,500 people, although that number could rise. Since the start of his second term, Trump has threatened to raise tariffs on Mexico if it did not impose greater complications and obstacles on Latin American migrants seeking to reach the United States across its borders. Since then, both countries have reached a series of agreements to more actively prevent migrants from crossing. Whether this is a genuine concern, a way to pressure Mexico, or a new tactic to win more votes, Trump’s statements regarding the arrival of migrants at the southern border have not gone unnoticed. Through economic threats, diplomatic pressure, and demands for military and intelligence cooperation, Trump has demanded that Mexican authorities detain migrants even before they reach the US border. In February 2025, Trump signed an additional 25% tariff increase on Mexican products, asserting that the Sheinbaum administration was not doing enough to prevent the arrival of migrants. In response, the Mexican government agreed to deploy 10,000 National Guard members to its northern border in exchange for the US increasing its controls on weapons entering Mexico from US territory, as well as the suspension of the extraordinary tariff measures. Mexico’s response In response to Trump’s threats regarding the migrant caravan heading toward the United States, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum sought to calm tensions and stated that “no migrant caravan has reached the [US] border.” However, the Mexican president clarified that there are indeed two migrant caravans: one in the south of the country, in Chiapas, and another that has recently begun to form in Honduras. Trump decided to use the migrant caravans to explain an alleged correlation between the arrival of migrants and the Democrats’ victory in the recent midterm elections: “The invasion of our country is happening again,” without providing any evidence to support that claim … “Huge caravans are forming and beginning their illegal march through Mexico.” In her statements to the press, Sheinbaum did not rule out a connection between the two events, but she warned that this is actually a scam used by human traffickers to convince people that they can now enter the United States, thereby charging them large sums of money. “It must be said that sometimes there are people who deceive migrants and tell them, for example, that the US election results have changed immigration policy, which is false,” Sheinbaum said. When asked about the possibility of pressure from migrants, Sheinbaum said that border authorities have significant experience dealing with these issues: “The vast majority [of migrants] return to their countries of origin once they realize that, well, they can’t – they won’t be able to – cross the Mexican-US border.” A caravan of dreams and hardships The group began its journey on November 15, crossing through Honduras and aiming to reach Guatemala. Among the migrants who left their homes for various reasons are men, women, and children seeking to reach US territory to start a new life. It is currently unknown what will happen to the caravan that has dubbed itself “God with Us.” El País reported that at least 300 people were dispersed by Mexican authorities, but that the bulk of the group continues to move forward at a slow pace. “We believe we can cross. The borders may be closed, but God can open the way for us,” said José Pérez , one of the migrants seeking work in the US. He added: “Our destination is New York; we’re going to try to cross the entire border – we don’t know where, but we’re going to get there.”

articles.title: Garment workers in Bangladesh resume protests for better minimum wages
articles.author: Abdul Rahman
articles.content: Security forces fired tear gas and stun grenades at thousands of workers protesting for better wages in Bangladesh’s capital, Dhaka, on the second consecutive day on Wednesday, November 18. The protesters, mostly women, marched across the city and blocked several roads, including the Dhaka-Meymensingh highway in and around the city and clashed with security forces setting their vehicles on fire at some places. Several workers were reportedly injured after the security forces’ crackdown. The security forces have also arrested scores of union leaders and agitating workers in the last two days accusing them of inciting violence. The large gathering of the workers on Wednesday forced some of the owners of garment factories to announce holidays while scores of other factories in Dhaka’s Gazipur area announced indefinite closure. The protests, which began last month over the demand for an increase in the monthly wages, were suspended earlier this month after the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP)-led government announced the formation of a Minimum Wage Board and promised to implement its recommendations from January 2027. At least one worker was killed and hundreds of others were injured in the state’s repressive actions in the earlier round of the protests. The repressive state actions had invited condemnation from human rights groups and World Federation of Trade Unions . Opposition parties and groups have also accused supporters of the ruling right-wing BNP of trying to malign the workers’ agitation and using its activists to unleash violence on them. The garment workers are demanding a raise in the minimum wages from the present 12,500 Bangladeshi Taka (around $100). Various groups have demanded the new minimum wage to be anywhere between 30,000 (around $240) to 37,127 (around $300). The workers claim that, instead of an increase, their real income has actually fallen drastically in the last three years due to the lack of revision in their wages, despite the rising cost of living and price of essential commodities and services. Bangladesh has witnessed constant high inflation in the last few years. In the last few months in particular due to the US-Israeli war on Iran. The economic situation of people across South Asia has further deteriorated as the supplies of the energy resources remain disrupted pushing the prices higher. The constant high prices of other essential commodities and services have made it difficult for most of the workers in the country to live a decent life on their present wages. Anger over delays in wage hikes The resumption of the protests on Tuesday is attributed to, what workers accused of, a deliberate delay by the factory owners association to submit responses to unions’ proposals for an increased monthly minimum wage in the earlier board meetings. The delay by the factory owners caused the postponement of the third scheduled meeting of the board on this Monday to November 23. Speaking to BreakThrough News , Shamshir Sharif, an activist with the Workers Party of Bangladesh (WPB) and academic also claimed that the fresh agitation may be a sign of widespread apprehensiveness among the workers about the motives of their representatives in the wage board. The workers fear that in the absence of the pressure from the streets the representatives may fail to push for their actual demand of the minimum wage of 30,000 Taka and settle for a token wage increase instead, Sharif argued. This is despite the fact that the union representatives have reportedly submitted a demand for 32,000 Taka monthly minimum wage. The union representatives claimed the 32,000 Taka benchmark was agreed after taking into consideration the industry’s capacity and the overall economic situation in the country despite the fact that the workers need a much higher wage to have a decent life for themselves and their dependents, Prothom Alo reported . Workers dismiss the concerns raised by the factory owners about the sustainability of a higher minimum wage pointing out how exports revenues and profits of the factories have risen in the last years. The garment workers are among the lowest paid workers in Bangladesh, despite the readymade garment export bringing around $39 billion to the country last year and being the largest source of the country’s foreign revenue (around 80%). Bangladesh is the second largest exporter of readymade garments in the world after China.

articles.title: Blue waves
articles.author: Sirantos Fotopoulos
articles.content: M illions of Americans delivered a well-deserved rebuke to Trump on Election Day, but the Democratic Party would be wise to resist the temptation to mistake an electorate’s hatred of Republican authoritarianism for an endorsement of corporate liberalism. The working class has spent forty years watching Democratic administrations convert blue waves into fresh mandates for the same economic establishment, and the historical record suggests that the only people likely to celebrate this victory without apprehension are the lobbyists, corporate donors, and political undertakers who have made a lucrative career out of burying popular expectations. The balance sheet on the last few blue waves The historical record is especially instructive because the U.S. has experienced several Democratic blue waves in recent decades, each accompanied by predictions of a new political settlement. In 1992, Bill Clinton arrived promising a different Democratic politics, supposedly capable of combining economic opportunity with social responsibility. What followed included the North American Free Trade Agreement, signed in 1993, and the 1996 Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act, which dismantled the existing federal welfare entitlement and replaced it with Temporary Assistance for Needy Families. Clinton subsequently signed legislation that imposed time limits and work requirements on assistance to poor families. The administration that had promised to make government work for ordinary Americans demonstrated considerable enthusiasm for making ordinary Americans accommodate the requirements of the market. The phrase “ending welfare as we know it” became an especially revealing description of the achievement. For working families, the consequences were considerably less amusing than the political marketing. Then came the Democratic victory of 2006, when widespread opposition to the Iraq War, Republican corruption, and the W. Bush administration’s economic policies delivered control of Congress to the Democrats. Nancy Pelosi became the first woman Speaker of the House, and the party promised a new direction for the country. Yet the political energy that had helped produce the victory was rapidly absorbed into the familiar routines of congressional management. The Iraq War continued, the financial system approached catastrophe, and the Democratic leadership demonstrated considerably more interest in restoring confidence among financial markets than in reorganizing the economic relationships that had produced the crisis. The wave had changed the occupants of congressional offices. It had yet to change the balance of power between capital and labor. The election of Barack Obama in 2008 produced perhaps the greatest expectations of any Democratic victory in modern American history. Millions believed that the 2008 financial catastrophe had finally discredited the economic establishment, that Wall Street would be forced to account for its conduct, and that working people would receive something resembling a New Deal for the twenty-first century. Obama inherited an extraordinary opportunity. His administration subsequently presided over the rescue and restructuring of the automobile industry, but the arrangement imposed substantial sacrifices on workers and retirees while preserving the corporate ownership structures that had helped produce the disaster. Shareholders and creditors absorbed losses, certainly, but autoworkers also faced plant closures, reduced employment, and the transfer of retiree healthcare obligations into a separate trust. The Employee Free Choice Act, which might have strengthened union organizing, died in Congress. Meanwhile, the financial system recovered with considerable assistance from public resources, while millions of households endured foreclosure, unemployment, and prolonged economic insecurity. The country received a historic president, Wall Street received a functioning rescue operation, and the working class was encouraged to regard recovery in the stock market as evidence of its own good fortune. The working class has spent forty years watching Democratic administrations convert blue waves into fresh mandates for the same economic establishment. The 2018 blue wave provides another useful exhibit. Democrats won 41 additional House seats, regained control of the chamber, and acquired a powerful institutional platform from which to challenge Trump’s administration. The result was politically important, and the subsequent investigations exposed serious abuses of presidential power. Yet the electoral victory produced little corresponding transformation in the economic organization of American society. Health care remained dominated by private insurers, labor protections remained inadequate, wealth concentration continued, and the basic relationship between corporate power and government survived largely intact. The Democratic leadership became increasingly adept at presenting the defense of constitutional institutions as a sufficient political program, even as millions of working people continued confronting stagnant wages, unaffordable housing, medical insecurity, and declining labor bargaining power. The 2020 Democratic victories were supposed to provide an especially decisive opportunity. Democrats controlled the presidency, the House, and the Senate, albeit with an exceptionally narrow Senate majority. There was a popular mandate for economic relief, and considerable public support for policies that would have materially improved working-class life. The $15 federal minimum wage proposal failed to survive the Senate’s procedural machinery. The PRO Act, which would have strengthened collective bargaining and workers’ organizing rights, failed to become law. The expanded Child Tax Credit, which had significantly reduced child poverty, expired after Congress declined to extend it. These were among the clearest illustrations of the distance between Democratic campaign promises and the actual distribution of political power within the party. The administration could accomplish important things, including substantial pandemic relief and infrastructure investment, but the interests of corporate America remained remarkably well represented throughout the process. A party capable of finding enormous resources when financial stability is threatened somehow discovers a more complicated set of constitutional and procedural difficulties when working people demand a larger share of national wealth. One might reasonably ask how many repetitions of this performance are required before the audience recognizes the production. The Democratic Party is a coalition, certainly, but its institutional leadership, major fundraising networks, and relationships with corporate America place formidable limits on its willingness to confront the ownership class. The party’s internal machinery remains deeply dependent upon wealthy donors, corporate fundraising, and the financial interests that dominate American politics. There are exceptions, insurgencies, and genuine reformers within its ranks. Yet the presence of progressive candidates on a Democratic ballot should never be confused with the political character of the institution they are attempting to change. Mass struggle, bourgeois parties, and the state The underlying question concerns the character of the state itself. In a capitalist society, government operates within an economic order whose commanding institutions remain overwhelmingly controlled by private owners. This gives capital enormous structural advantages, including the ability to influence economic conditions upon which elected governments depend. Yet the state is also a terrain of political struggle, and the history of labor movements demonstrates that organized people can force governments and employers to concede ground. The New Deal, the civil rights movement, the labor struggles of the twentieth century, and the expansion of social protections were achieved through combinations of political mass mobilization, economic disruption, and sustained popular pressure which at times included violent riots. The lesson is considerably more interesting than the parliamentary procedural romanticism of the Democratic establishment. A tenant union that prevents an eviction has altered the immediate balance of power between a landlord and a family. Workers who organize a credible strike have established a capacity to interrupt production and impose costs upon an employer. A neighborhood organization that mobilizes legal assistance, public solidarity, and material support against deportation has created a practical obstacle to the machinery of state coercion. These organizations possess something that campaign advertisements and congressional press conferences cannot manufacture: the capacity to make powerful interests confront consequences. Their achievements may eventually require legislation, but their initial strength comes from people acting collectively rather than waiting for permission from political representatives. The ballot can help create favorable conditions for such organization. It cannot substitute for it. The Democratic leadership will undoubtedly describe election 2026 as a historic mandate. The corporate donors will congratulate the party on its impressive performance. The television networks will discover a new collection of political personalities, and Washington will begin its elaborate ritual of interpreting electoral arithmetic as a substitute for social analysis. Meanwhile, the people who voted against Trump will return to work, pay their rent, confront their medical bills, worry about their children’s futures, and discover whether their political victory has improved the material conditions of their lives. They should demand evidence rather than expressions of gratitude. They should measure the incoming majority by wages raised, unions strengthened, housing made affordable, public services expanded, detention budgets challenged, and corporate privileges withdrawn. Another new blue wave can also become another episode in the long history of American electoral disappointment, where popular anger is converted into institutional legitimacy and the people who supplied the votes are subsequently invited to admire the wisdom of their representatives. The difference will be determined by what happens after the election, when the cameras depart and the lobbyists return to their offices. The working class has already supplied the votes. The incoming majority now has an opportunity to demonstrate what those votes were worth. But the decisive question belongs to the people themselves: whether they intend to remain an electoral constituency periodically summoned to rescue the Democratic Party from the abyss, or become an organized political force capable of making the entire political establishment answer to them. Four chances for the Democrats to disappoint The historical record explains where the party has failed before, and the coming years supply the occasions on which it may fail again, with consequences that reach well beyond the next set of primaries. The danger lies less in Democratic incompetence than in Democratic competence, because the party is extraordinarily skilled at the task its donors require of it, which is to stabilize the existing order at the moment that order is threatened. Each stabilization leaves a payment still due, the outstanding bill lands on the people who voted for the Democrats, and the demagogues of the next cycle are generous in their willingness to read the invoice aloud. Consider the artificial intelligence boom, which has become the largest debt-financed building campaign in modern corporate history. The five largest firms will have spent roughly $800 billion on capital projects in 2026 and are expected to approach $1.1 trillion in 2027, while borrowing for the buildout now accounts for around 30 percent of net investment-grade bond issuance Pension funds and insurers hold much of the paper. If revenue fails to arrive on schedule, the losses will be shifted to retirement savings and municipal budgets, and that route determines what any bailout rescue will be called. The party that controls both chambers will then face a choice its history has already answered. Leadership will describe the bailout as protection for pensioners, workers, and the municipalities that borrowed against promised data center revenue, and the description will carry a measure of truth, because the exposure is genuine. Yet the guarantee will flow to the executives, bondholders, and lenders who designed the structure, and it will arrive without equity stakes, without limits on compensation, without the breakup of any monopoly, and without a single protection for the households that lose their jobs or their homes while the markets recover. The sequence repeats 2008 with the labels changed, and the party that performs it will have spent public credit to preserve private ownership in the very industry whose lobbyists helped finance its campaigns. The Musks, Zuckerbergs, and Bezoses were once aligned with the Nancy Pelosi and Kamala Harris class before they swung their pendulum towards Trump. They will now swing towards the new Democratic Congressional leadership. It is in their interest to do so. No parasite can survive without a host. And, when the host dies, a new host must be pursued. The billionaire who has spent a career protecting his own fortune will campaign as the enemy of billionaires, and the evidence will be supplied by the Democratic leadership itself. No party survives in office whose voters are failed repeatedly while being told that the cure for failure is a larger turnout. The affordability crisis offers a second occasion for the party to disappoint its voters. The war with Iran, launched in late February without a declaration of Congress, has pushed crude oil above $100 a barrel, raised the costs of farming, trucking, and heating, and could add roughly half a percentage point to inflation in the first quarter of 2027, according to a Congressional Budget Office estimate. The House has passed a war powers resolution 3 times, and the Senate has voted on such a measure 14 times without ending the war, so the legislative record already shows what a resolution accomplishes against a president who vetoes it and a chamber that lacks the two-thirds majority required to override him. Democratic leaders will therefore hold a majority, a war, and a price level, with only one instrument capable of changing the first two, which is the power over appropriations. They will decline to use it, because every strategist in the party will warn that limits on war funding invite the charge of abandoning the troops and defying AIPAC, and the same strategists will advise against anything that hands the Right a slogan for 2028. Prices will remain high, and voters who have just been told that Democrats will come to the rescue will feel abandoned yet again. The most dangerous feature of the coming cycle is that the Right’s indictment [of the Democrats] will contain accurate claims. A third occasion arises in the budget itself. Appropriations bills carry the funding for detention, deportation, and military procurement alongside the funding for schools and hospitals, and leadership has a long habit of accepting the former in exchange for the latter. Hearings will expose abuses, officials will snub subpoenas, and the spending lines will be renewed anyway on the argument that a government shutdown would punish the vulnerable. The same vote that finances the machinery will be cited, correctly, by every organizer who is asked why the people who knocked on doors for the majority should knock again in 2028. A fourth chance for the Democrats to disappoint its voters lies in the politics of electricity and shelter. State legislatures controlled by Democrats will compete to attract data centers with tax abatements and discounted power contracts, and the households in those states will face higher utility bills, while the promised jobs prove to be a few hundred technicians at each site. Meanwhile the federal bills that would raise wages and strengthen unions will die behind the filibuster, as they did five years ago, and leadership will blame procedural obstacles—with sorrow and regret. Taken together, these occasions explain how the pendulum swings. No party survives in office whose voters are failed repeatedly while being told that the cure for failure is a larger turnout. The voters who supplied the majority will conclude, with considerable justification, that elections change the faces administering their circumstances and leave the circumstances intact. Some will withdraw into private exhaustion, while others, a crucial minority, will turn toward whichever movement offers an explanation for their suffering, and the authoritarian Right has never lacked explanations, since its explanations demand neither evidence nor accountability. A movement of the discarded must be organized by the discarded themselves, or it will be organized against them. The most dangerous feature of the coming cycle is that the Right’s indictment will contain accurate claims. Every claim that Democrats rescued the powerful, prolonged the costs of the war, and funded the ICE machinery they condemned will be demonstrable from the congressional record, and the demagogue who delivers those claims will pair them with an invented culprit, because a true grievance married to a false enemy is the oldest instrument in the authoritarian repertoire. A movement of the discarded must be organized by the discarded themselves, or it will be organized against them. Trump was defeated by a country that remembered what it had been promised and discovered it was still capable of collective refusal. That memory is now the most valuable and most perishable resource in American politics, and the Democratic Party holds it in trust with no evident intention of spending it on the people who deposited it. If the majority uses the memory to rescue the financiers of the next decade, to administer the costs of a war it declined to stop, and to fund the machinery it promised to investigate, then the country will learn in 2028 that the hand raised against the old authoritarianism can be raised for a new form of rule. The wave will have delivered what the owners wanted all along, which is a pause, and the pause will have been purchased with the patience of everyone who believed it was a beginning. Only an organized people can make it a beginning, and the hour for organizing arrives while the wave still stands, before the water finds its level. The Democrats are riding into office on a wave of popular revolt against tyranny, but the party will take every chance to disappoint—unless the struggle is organized to continue. articles.title: A New International Order? Xi, Trump & Putin Hold Historic Trilateral Summit in China
articles.content: This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. NERMEEN SHAIKH : We begin today’s show looking at today’s historic trilateral summit in China between Chinese President Xi Jinping, President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin. The three leaders met for about 90 minutes. After the meeting, Chinese state media issued what it described as a, quote, “peace declaration” by the Chinese, Russian and U.S. leaders. The four-point declaration called for reforms at the United Nations and said the three leaders, quote, “concurred that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction.” The three countries are not signatories to the ICC . The ICC has issued an arrest warrant for Putin for war crimes committed in Ukraine. The declaration also states, quote, “The three countries plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations.” In addition, the declaration states, quote, “The three countries will engage in dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing nuclear proliferation.” AMY GOODMAN : Prior to the closed-door meeting, the three leaders shared brief remarks. This is Chinese President Xi Jinping. PRESIDENT XI JINPING : [translated] This is the first time the leaders of our three countries have come together. It is a historic meeting. We will discuss how to safeguard world peace and promote strategic stability and relations among major powers. … The world is undergoing rapid changes unseen in a century. The world is not peaceful, and challenges reveal true leadership. As major world powers and permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, our three nations should lead by example, collaborate to address global challenges, jointly safeguard world peace and stability, and make more significant contributions to the progress of humanity. AMY GOODMAN : Russian President Vladimir Putin also spoke before the trilateral meeting in China. PRESIDENT VLADIMIR PUTIN : [translated] For my part, I am convinced that Russia, China and the United States, and our respective peoples, are capable of making a significant contribution to strengthening global security and stability, provided they engage in constructive, partnership-based cooperation rooted in mutual respect, equality and a balance of interests. NERMEEN SHAIKH : And this is President Trump speaking in China before the trilateral meeting. PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP : As presidents of three of the world’s largest countries, we have a special responsibility to maintain open, respectful and productive dialogue on issues impacting not just our people, but the entire planet. Too often past leaders avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements. And we feel the opposite, and we think that we are sure about that. No problems were ever solved under the old school refusing to talk about them, so no peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech. AMY GOODMAN : Well, we’re joined right now by Scott Lucas. He’s a professor of international politics at University College Dublin’s Clinton Institute. Professor Lucas, thanks so much for being with us. First, if you can just talk about the significance of this moment, of these three world leaders coming together for the first time ever in China, President Trump, the Russian President Vladimir Putin, as well as the Chinese President Xi Jinping? SCOTT LUCAS : Well, Amy, I think it’s a significant post-1945 moment, which was, you know, the last time that we had great summits, including discussing the future of China, in part because you’re looking at a changed international order. You’re looking at a United States which is no longer the leader of that post-1945 system. You’re looking at a Russia having succeeded the Soviet Union, which is very much tied down by this struggling invasion of Ukraine, now in its fifth year, isolated, in some part, economically and politically because of that invasion, struggling to escape that isolation. And you’re looking at, I think, what is the most important takeaway, both symbolically and in real terms, from the summit, which is an ascendant China. It was China that really set the terms of what was said throughout this, beyond Ukraine, talking more about the global situation in a couple of ways. They did that symbolically by putting Xi right at the center, as you saw at that table, between Putin and Trump. China now is a great power. But they also did it with the specific terms that they put forward: strategic stability, unity, technology and innovation, and perhaps most striking, free trade — given that, of course, the United States had premised its post-1945 position on precisely that, but you have a Trump administration doing something much differently. There’s a lot of specific takeaways, especially because Donald — because Putin’s priority was Ukraine, but this was a summit where you had Trump coming there for ego and the photo opportunity, Putin because of the problems with his invasion and trying to get an alliance with Trump to force Ukraine’s surrender, and China there for strategy, a political, economic and military free hand in pursuing its alternative system. NERMEEN SHAIKH : Well, Professor Lucas, could you comment specifically on some of the remarks that were made by these leaders, what we mentioned in our introduction on the International Criminal Court, as well as — you know, we’re speaking to you — we’re here at COP31 at the U.N. climate summit in Antalya, Turkey — this pledge that they would all increase petroleum production? SCOTT LUCAS : So, one of the features where we are now, with the post-1945 system breaking, perhaps broken, is the dismissal of international law. And that is what you saw, on camera, before that closed-door meeting. Vladimir Putin is wanted on war crimes charges, specifically the deportation of Ukrainian children, by the International Criminal Court. He does not want to face those charges. Donald Trump, who wants a friendship with Vladimir Putin, who will be shown in that vivid embrace of Putin — “He is my friend” — was there to carry out Putin’s wishes by saying the International Criminal Court should have no credibility — not even that its decisions can be questioned, it has no credibility. So, that is where we are, between two of the three leading powers, that there is no regard for the International Criminal Court. And the Chinese, of course, have sort of a different approach, because they’re looking for a different type of international system. I think whether you’re at COP31 dealing with specific questions of climate change, or you’re dealing with specific questions of war crimes or broader questions of justice, this is a crisis moment for international law and for the ICC . NERMEEN SHAIKH : And could you comment also on the fact that this meeting comes so soon after Jensen Huang, the chief of Nvidia, was forced to step down after reports of his affair with an alleged Chinese spy, in addition to two others in his company? Do you think that’s significant at all? And would it have come up? SCOTT LUCAS : I don’t think it would have come up directly, but I think it’s part of the important backdrop at work here, which is, on the one hand, China is working from a position of leverage — of course, we’ve known this for quite some time — with its possession of rare earth minerals, with its dominance in terms of magnets. But, of course, it needs chips. On the other side, you have a Trump administration which is almost in chaos right now for two very important reasons. First of all, American companies, in this case Nvidia, allegedly, was taking 20% of its revenue from China, despite saying that none of it came from there. Now, that’s a specific gap regarding where you are in terms of AI and technology in the U.S.-versus-China relationship. And that is magnified by the revelation that the Commerce Department did not enforce more than 100 recommended export controls on China-linked firms. So, on the one hand, you have China, which has a very clear policy where it wants to go with tech and AI and with innovation and with control of resources, and you have a Trump administration that’s scrambling and divided over where exactly its position is right now in terms of the relationship with China. Open supply of chips? Export controls? Something in between? Where does it go next? AMY GOODMAN : I also wanted to ask you — at the same time that they’re meeting in Shenzhen in China, Putin and Xi and Trump, you have Jared Kushner and Witkoff meeting with President Zelensky, with other European representatives. The significance of this and what this means? SCOTT LUCAS : There are two different agendas right now in terms of where we go next regarding that invasion of Ukraine. The Russian agenda is to push Ukraine to the side — don’t discuss a ceasefire, don’t discuss security guarantees for Kyiv, don’t discuss freezing the frontlines; instead, call for a Europe-wide security architecture, by which the Russians mean security guarantees for us, and NATO withdrawing to its 1997 position, which not only means, of course, that Ukraine is exposed. It means that there’s no NATO , effectively, in the Baltic states or in Poland. On the other hand, you have Ukraine and Europe that are saying, “No. Before you discuss a European-wide security arrangement, you need to have a specific commitment to a ceasefire on the current frontlines. You need to have an agreement that Russia will not get more territory. And you need to have security guarantees for Kyiv, so we don’t have a repeat of this aggression.” The problem that we have right now is, is that the Russians are trying to impose their agenda by putting Donald Trump in their pocket. How are they doing that? You saw part of it today from Putin’s rhetoric, and from Trump supporting that rhetoric. But perhaps more seriously, you have it through the Russians putting tens of billions of dollars of proposed economic deals on the table, including some deals that would benefit friends and family of Donald Trump and his envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, and saying, “You can get all these deals, provided this invasion is halted on our terms.” AMY GOODMAN : Let me ask you something, and this last question: On the one hand, you have President Trump announcing there shouldn’t be regulation of SI, what he calls superintelligence, but also, will this set a new template for the international order, major powers meeting amongst themselves, ignoring the U.N. Security Council and other forums? We just have a minute, Professor Lucas. SCOTT LUCAS : First of all, Trump’s statement, supported by some of the people in the technological industry, is: “Look, don’t restrict us. Don’t do anything to restrict what we’re doing with AI.” More broadly, what you’re seeing here is this isn’t a question of international order. International order has broken down because certain countries and certain leaders don’t believe in international order. I think that’s true of Vladimir Putin. And with regret, I think that’s also true of Donald Trump and his inner circle. But I think the country that benefits from that lack of respect for international order, and we saw it today, is China. AMY GOODMAN : Professor Scott Lucas teaches international politics at the Clinton Institute, University College Dublin. Coming up, we’re going to go here to Turkey to summarize what’s happening at the U.N. climate summit, in the plenaries, but also outside, where all sorts of groups are protesting all the issues that are being discussed here. Stay with us. [break] AMY GOODMAN : “The Fire of Antalya,” performed at the COP31 opening ceremony. Page 2 This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. AMY GOODMAN : This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman, with Nermeen Shaikh. We’re broadcasting from Antalya, Turkey, at the global U.N. climate summit, known as COP31. NERMEEN SHAIKH : As we reach the final hours of climate negotiations at this global conference, negotiators have released a second draft text for the final outcome of this year’s COP . Global civil society activists have already criticized the text for stripping out hard-won language on accountability from Global North countries and legal anchors to protect the countries and communities most vulnerable to climate change. AMY GOODMAN : Earlier today, Teresa Anderson, the global lead on climate justice at ActionAid International, said climate negotiations are, quote, “looking bleak.” She criticized the European Union’s climate chief Wopke Hoekstra. TERESA ANDERSON : Before coming to COP , actually, the EU’s climate chief, Hoekstra, said any chance of a deal on new climate finance is “dead in the water.” “Dead in the water.” The more I think about it, the more shocked I am that he used that term, in the aftermath of Nepal, as El Niño floods are happening. I’m shocked that he chose that metaphor. When the next catastrophic flood happens, those words will haunt him. NERMEEN SHAIKH : Democracy Now! also caught up with campaigners who’ve been closely following the negotiations here at COP31. This is Kirtana Chandrasekaran from Friends of the Earth International speaking alongside a protest for just solutions from wealthy countries in the Global North. PROTESTERS : No false solutions! Real solutions now! Real solutions now! No false solutions! No false solutions! KIRTANA CHANDRASEKARAN : I’m Kirtana Chandrasekaran with Friends of the Earth International. I was at the “divan” meeting last night, and the divan is supposed to be a roundtable for leaders, but there was no leadership in the room. And all we saw is the Global North countries abandoning their moral and legal commitments, country after country saying that “we are worried about breaching 1.5,” with no irony about how we’ve got here, which is 30 years of inaction on their part, and the solution for that being so-called clean electrification. And what we can see happening now, under the guise of clean electrification, we are seeing many, many new gas plants to electrify data centers. We are seeing many, many new coal plants in the Global South, a massive push, and nuclear, as well. So, they say the words, but they’re not doing any of it. And so they talk about roadmaps, but what is in the roadmap? You know, they were supposed to mobilize $100 million. If you talk about clean electrification, it requires over $2 trillion of investment just for grids and electricity. AMY GOODMAN : At another protest just this morning, a young activist from Nepal urged people to visit her country to experience what it’s like to live on the frontlines of a climate change-fueled catastrophe. SNEHA RAI : I think everybody here knows about the 26th August, 2026, flood. … This is not a single disaster. I think this is the one disaster that you have reached to you on the further side of the world. But we have been facing this on yearly. Yearly, every year, we have been facing this. We don’t need hope anymore. We don’t need words anymore. We need actions right now. And Nepal is a mountainous country, you know, and we have been saying that we are resilient people. We are resilient, but there is a limit to resilient. AMY GOODMAN : Just some of the voices here at the U.N. climate summit. For more, we’re joined by Luisa Neubauer. She is a climate justice activist, lead organizer of Germany’s Fridays for Future movement. In 2021, she was the lead plaintiff in the landmark Neubauer v. Germany case, which forced the German government to strengthen its national climate protection laws. We welcome you to Democracy Now! here at the U.N. climate summit. Right now as we’re sitting here, the second draft of the — for the final report here has just come out. And I’m wondering if you can talk about the progress that has been made, and not made, what you’re most concerned about, Luisa. LUISA NEUBAUER : Yes, of course. So, this is a conference where we try to solve our existential climate problems. And we do know, we are all aware, that the root cause of that very problem is oil, coal and gas. That’s the fossil fuels. So, now we are faced with a new draft negotiation text where the mention of having to get away from the use and exploitation of oil, coal and gas is being stripped out. So, what are we talking about then? And then, what we do see in the text, which is included, is that Saudi Arabia and some petroleum states have really won big time here, because suddenly there’s inclusion of, I would say, magic technologies sucking CO2 out of the atmosphere, which is mentioned big times. We do know those technologies won’t deliver in scale. We have much better solutions at hand, like renewables. So, we see, really, this is not going well. We are not doing fine. And if anything, after this conference ends, we need people to take the streets and fight for more justice out there. NERMEEN SHAIKH : And also, I mean, you mentioned Saudi Arabia and all these petroleum-producing states. Talk about the IPCC report — LUISA NEUBAUER : Yes. NERMEEN SHAIKH : — which has now been delayed. And what justification was given for its delay? LUISA NEUBAUER : It is a real achievement that everything that is being discussed here in these halls is based on the best available science. That is something people have fought for. It’s a real achievement. And now we’ve seen in recent months that some of the most powerful countries, including the U.S., have been very vocal about kind of boycotting the involvement in the climate science here in these halls. But that means the doors are wide open for all kinds of denial and relativation of what we are seeing here. So, now in the new negotiation text, there is a better, I would say, agreement that we have to have the science in the room, which you can call a achievement. But for me, honestly, that’s a bare minimum. I mean, what are we talking about? If this is about discussing should we have climate science in the room or not, what are we even aiming at? NERMEEN SHAIKH : And, you know, you are from Germany and were one of the lead organizers of the Fridays for Future in Germany. Could you tell us why Germany has changed? It was, as you’ve pointed out, also a climate pioneer. LUISA NEUBAUER : Yeah. NERMEEN SHAIKH : And now it seems to have altered its position, and also, in fact, the entire EU no longer stands where it once did. LUISA NEUBAUER : Yeah. articles.title: Russian Indigenous Activist Daria Egereva Remains Jailed; Arrested After 2025 U.N. Climate Talks
articles.content: Human rights and climate groups are calling on Russia to release two prominent activists, Daria Egereva and Natalia Leongardt, who have been held in pretrial detention in Moscow for nearly a year, since December 2025. Egereva, a leading Indigenous rights activist in Russia, was arrested shortly after attending the COP30 United Nations climate summit in Belém, Brazil, where she served as co-chair of the International Indigenous Peoples Forum on Climate Change. Leongardt has worked for decades to support Indigenous rights. “Right now all we are demanding is the release of Daria and Natalia, because they shouldn’t be in prison. You shouldn’t be arrested for activism,” says Viktor Suliandziga-Bagat, an Indigenous rights activist and representative of the Udege people from the Russian Far East. He is living in exile due to the risk against activists. “I don’t think I can come back to Russia,” he says.
