articles.title: El regreso de las bases: por qué los filipinos luchan contra la Pax Silica
articles.author: Atul Chandra
articles.content: Read in English here El domingo, mientras los líderes del sudeste asiático se reunían en Manila para la 49 Cumbre de la ASEAN, la policía filipina llevó a cabo lo que los activistas denominan la mayor redada en un solo día en décadas de la presidencia de Ferdinand Marcos Jr. En el Parque del Pueblo de Sucat, en Muntinlupa – un parque designado como espacio de libertad –, la policía detuvo a más de 300 personas. Otras ocho fueron detenidas en Liwasang Bonifacio, en Manila, mientras intentaban marchar hacia la sede de la cumbre. Las imágenes de televisión mostraron a la policía arrestándolas y deteniéndolas de manera brutal . El Sindicato Nacional de Periodistas de Filipinas (NUJP) afirma que al menos 22 trabajadores de los medios de comunicación que cubrían las protestas fueron acosados . ¿Quiénes eran ellos ? Campesinos, estudiantes, pueblos indígenas y trabajadores. Lo que los unía era una exigencia que el invitado de honor de la Conferencia de la ASEAN preferiría no escuchar: acaben con la Pax Silica. El presidente Donald Trump aterriza en Manila el martes 17 de noviembre de 2026. Se trata de su primera visita desde 2017, y se han desplegado cerca de 20.000 agentes de policía en toda la capital para recibirlo a él y a otros líderes de la ASEAN. Se espera que presione a los gobiernos del sudeste asiático para que se unan a la Pax Silica. Para comprender por qué tantos filipinos están dispuestos a ser arrestados para detenerla, debemos remontarnos a 1991. Ese año, el Senado filipino hizo algo que pocas naciones pequeñas se atreven a hacer. Votó a favor de poner fin al Tratado de Amistad, Cooperación y Seguridad que permitía a los Estados Unidos mantener bases militares en territorio filipino. Ese mismo año, el volcán Pinatubo entró en erupción y sepultó la Base Aérea de Clark bajo cenizas. Para finales de 1992, los últimos buques de guerra estadounidenses habían zarpado de la Bahía de Subic. Durante una generación, los filipinos contaron esta historia con orgullo. Las bases habían desaparecido. Treinta y cinco años después, los estadounidenses regresan a Clark. Esta vez traen consigo centros de datos. El primer proyecto físico de Pax Silica es un centro industrial de inteligencia artificial de aproximadamente alrededor de 4000 acres en el Corredor Económico de Luzón, ubicado en parte de la antigua base aérea de Clark. Bajo la presión de las protestas callejeras, el embajador de los Estados Unidos en Filipinas, Lee Lipton, afirma ahora que no se hará ningún anuncio en la cumbre, y Manila espera firmar el acuerdo antes de que termine el año. El acuerdo se ha retrasado. Las detenciones del domingo demuestran hasta dónde está dispuesto a llegar el gobierno para mantenerlo vivo. Una paz escrita en Washington El Departamento de Estado de los EE. UU. lanzó Pax Silica en diciembre de 2025. Reúne a los países clave en la “pila de silicio”: las minas, las centrales eléctricas, las fábricas de chips, los centros de cómputo y los modelos de inteligencia artificial sobre los que funciona la economía digital. Aproximadamente dos docenas de gobiernos se han sumado, desde Japón y Corea del Sur hasta India, Israel y Kazajistán. El nombre no es casualidad. La Pax Romana fue la larga “paz romana” que comenzó en el año 27 a. C., impuesta al mundo mediterráneo por las legiones de Roma y financiada con los tributos de las provincias conquistadas. La Pax Britannica fue el siglo posterior a 1815, cuando la Marina Real dominaba los mares y el imperio británico se extendía desde la India hasta África. La Pax Americana es el orden que los Estados Unidos construyó después de 1945, basado en el dólar y en cientos de bases militares alrededor del mundo. Quienes se encontraban en el centro llamaban a cada uno de ellos “paz”. Para quienes estaban en los márgenes, significaban conquista, saqueo y guerras libradas lejos de la capital imperial. La Pax Silica reclama abiertamente un lugar en esta línea. El hombre que la ideó es Jacob Helberg, subsecretario de Asuntos Económicos del Departamento de Estado. Antes de asumir el cargo, fue asesor principal del director ejecutivo de Palantir, la empresa que desarrolla software de vigilancia y selección de objetivos para ejércitos y agencias de espionaje. La Pax Silica nació en la encrucijada entre Silicon Valley y el Estado de seguridad. La versión oficial es que Pax Silica protege las cadenas de suministro frente a China, como lo evidencia el término “dependencias coercitivas”. Este argumento cobró mayor fuerza con el informe de Reuters que reveló un borrador de carta del Departamento de Estado dirigida a 35 países en la que se les advertía contra “iniciativas duplicadas cuyas expectativas entren en conflicto con las nuestras”. Las condiciones de lealtad son estrictas. El objetivo inmediato es la nueva Organización Mundial de Cooperación en Inteligencia Artificial (WAICO) de China. Pero el mensaje llega a todos los socios. Sus decisiones ya no le pertenecen por completo. Se trata de la vieja política del Estado cliente, reescrita para la era de la IA. Eso es parte de la verdad, pero solo una parte. Su propósito más profundo es decidir quién controla las tecnologías del próximo siglo y bajo qué condiciones. Dentro del bloque, los roles ya están definidos. Washington y sus gigantes tecnológicos conservan los modelos de IA más avanzados, redactan las normas y tienen el control de apagado. Los socios aportan la tierra, el agua, los minerales y la mano de obra. Los críticos advierten que esto crea una trampa de “ interdependencia de confianza ”. El regreso de las bases Regresemos ahora a Clark y observemos el mapa que lo rodea. El puerto de la Bahía de Subic, que alguna vez fue una de las mayores bases navales estadounidenses en el extranjero, ha sido designado como la puerta de entrada marítima oficial de la Pax Silica. Más al norte se encuentran las instalaciones militares que las fuerzas estadounidenses utilizan en virtud del Acuerdo de Cooperación de Defensa Mejorada . Actualmente hay nueve de ellas. Desde abril de 2024 se encuentra estacionado en Luzón un sistema de misiles de alcance medio Typhon de los EE. UU., y durante los ejercicios militares Balikatan de este año se instalaron lanza misiles antibuque estadounidenses en una de estas instalaciones. Las autoridades filipinas insisten en que el centro de inteligencia artificial es puramente comercial . Pero es difícil separar el comercio de la guerra cuando los productos son chips y minerales críticos. Las tierras raras guían los misiles. Los semiconductores hacen volar los drones y operan los radares. Las nuevas normas de Manila sobre minerales críticos podrían abrir alrededor de nueve millones de hectáreas a la exploración minera. Es por eso que la alianza popular BAYAN denomina a la “Pax Silica# como producción bélica disfrazada de desarrollo. China es el rival obvio en este plan, y Washington no lo oculta. Sin embargo, la lógica del imperio va más allá de cualquier rival en particular. Los Estados Unidos desea que la tierra, la mano de obra, los minerales y la lealtad de Asia se organicen en torno a su propia industria armamentística y a sus monopolios tecnológicos, sea cual sea el enemigo del momento. La lista de miembros lo refleja. Israel, uno de los signatarios fundadores, ha utilizado sistemas de puntería con IA en su guerra contra Gaza. Kazajistán posee una vasta riqueza mineral en la frontera occidental de China. Singapur custodia el Estrecho de Malaca. No se trata simplemente de mercados. Son puntos estratégicos, minas y frentes de batalla. ¿Quién paga el precio? El precio lo está pagando primero Tarlac. Según se ha informado, en la aldea de Sapang Kawayan, unas 200 familias aeta han recibido cartas de la empresa estatal de desarrollo en las que se les indica que deben reubicarse. Los aeta son el pueblo indígena de las estribaciones del Pinatubo, y muchos ya fueron expulsados de sus hogares una vez por la erupción de 1991. “Más vale que nos maten, porque lucharemos por nuestra tierra”, afirmó Casamira Capiz Maniego, de 72 años. La Autoridad de Conversión y Desarrollo de Bases (BCDA) insiste en que solo 40 hogares se ven afectados y que nadie “será desplazado”. La tierra es solo el comienzo. Según Mongabay , el centro necesitaría alrededor de 3 gigavatios de electricidad y entre 60 y 90 millones de litros de agua al día. Los filipinos ya pagan las tarifas de electricidad residencial más altas del sudeste asiático. Los agricultores de la zona temen por su suministro de agua durante la estación seca, y los grupos ambientalistas señalan que las autoridades no han presentado ningún estudio hidrológico . La oposición ahora va mucho más allá de la izquierda. Cáritas Filipinas, el brazo de acción social de la Iglesia Católica, se opone al centro en su forma actual. El obispo Gerardo Alminaza afirma que el proyecto se está llevando a cabo con prisas, con muy pocas consultas con los aeta. El alcalde de Capas, la localidad que albergaría el centro, afirma que nunca se consultó a los funcionarios locales. Cuando falta la consulta, la coacción ocupa su lugar. En septiembre, la policía arrestó a cinco asistentes legales y detuvo a casi 30 personas frente a un hotel donde se celebraba un foro de Pax Silica. Las detenciones masivas del domingo siguen el mismo patrón, pero a mayor escala. Un imperio que necesita tierras baratas y comunidades tranquilas en el extranjero también necesita gobiernos dispuestos a silenciar a su propio pueblo. Este es el viejo pacto del imperio con un nuevo ropaje. La tierra, el agua y la mano de obra provienen del Sur. Las ganancias, las patentes y el poder se quedan en el Norte. Nada de esto significa que el Sur Global deba darle la espalda a la tecnología. Los países en desarrollo necesitan chips e inteligencia artificial. Pero los necesitan en sus propios términos, a través de la transferencia de tecnología, la inversión pública y la cooperación entre ellos, y con el consentimiento de las comunidades cuyas tierras y aguas están en juego. Pax Silica no ofrece nada de esto. El sudeste asiático sabe que es posible negarse. De los once miembros de la ASEAN, solo Singapur y Filipinas se han sumado a la iniciativa . En 1991, los filipinos demostraron al mundo que las bases extranjeras podían ser expulsadas. Los agricultores, los estudiantes y los aeta que llenaron las cárceles de la zona metropolitana de Manila el domingo están dando continuidad a ese recuerdo. No están en contra de la tecnología. Están en contra de que los conviertan en la materia prima del imperio de otros. Atul Chandra es uno de los coordinadores para Asia de Tricontinental: Instituto de Investigación Social. Este artículo fue elaborado por Globetrotter .

articles.title: Healthcare workers respond to a broken system by unionizing
articles.author: Dennis Kosuth
articles.content: C hicago is seeing a burst of unionization amongst registered nurses – and it has become infectious, in the best sense of that word. In May of 2026, 77 percent of nurses at Rush University Medical Center (RUMC) voted in favor of joining the National Nurses Organizing Committee (NNOC). The 1,700 nurses at RUMC are now part of National Nurses United (NNU), a union that represents 225,000 nurses in healthcare settings across the United States. NNU was founded by a merger of nursing unions in 2009 and, in the past 17 years,has grown considerably from its initial strength of 150,000. The latest victory for NNOC took place in the first week of November when nurses who work for Endeavor Health at Edward Hospital in suburban Naperville, voted by a margin of 65 percent in favor of joining the union. By adding another 1,200 nurses to the Chicagoland area, NNOC now represents over 10,000 members in the region. Nurses at Chicago’s Saint Mary of Nazareth Hospital voted 96 percent in favor of unionizing in June of 2026 – days after going on a one-day strike six days before the vote had even occurred- over the unlawful termination of nurses who were advocating for having a collective voice in their workplace. St. Mary Hospital was acquired by Prime Healthcare in March of 2025, and nurses were motivated to take action following drastic changes they experienced in patient care, following cost-cutting measures taken by Prime to boost their bottom line. Nurses at St. Mary struck again for one day on September 3. On September 15, nurses at Olympia Fields Hospital in suburban Chicago, also owned by Prime Healthcare, went on a one-day strike, also voting with an 82 percent margin to join the union about a week afterwards, adding another 400 nurses to NNOC. In early December, 2,400 nurses at four hospitals in the northern Chicago suburbs owned by Endeavor will have an opportunity to vote to organize with Teamsters Union Local 743. Across the United States, there are almost 4.5 million registered nurses, and about one in five of them are in unions – double the overall unionization rate of workers in this country. There are various factors at play behind these statistics, with the most notable ones being a response to chronic understaffing, post-COVID pandemic exhaustion, and the leverage that comes with the relatively higher job security that nurses have. I am a NNOC member, a nurse who works part-time at Cook County’s Stroger hospital, and recently was in conversation with three nurses from St. Mary Hospital and one nurse from RUMC. They had all led successful campaigns to unionize their hospitals with NNOC in the spring of 2026. The testimony of these nurses is useful for understanding what is pushing nurses to organize themselves, the challenges they are confronting in these campaigns, and what the future holds for healthcare workers fighting for justice. Mary, a nurse who works at RUMC, reported on how her coworkers joined the organizing campaign at St. Mary, on the heels of the RUMC vote to join NNOC. She said, “The most inspiring thing was seeing nurses come together for St. Mary’s. It came at the perfect time for us because everyone was so hyped up and excited and ready to jump into action. Seeing people [at RUMC] commit the time, not just for ourselves, but for other nurses in the community to make all nurses in Chicago, and the country, to make work better for them – was really inspiring.” Working conditions were a major driver of nurse unionization. Richard, a nurse at St. Mary, described what motivated him to organize after Prime took over. “Things just got worse and worse. One of the things that happened is my coworker got his ribs broken and he got a black eye from being beaten really badly by a patient because we weren’t staffed properly. I just wanted to be able to have them give us a proper amount of staff under whatever circumstances we have, rather than just applying to some basic rule of one staff to six patients.” Patient safety was a big concern for Jesús, also a nurse at St. Mary, as the employer didn’t want to have “sitters,” someone to watch patients to prevent falls. His unit has “a lot of geriatric dementia patients, and Prime wanted them to be without a sitter, and they were pushing us to admit these patients without one. You can’t really say that patients need a sitter right away, but you’ve seen enough falls and enough adverse complications from falls to know who needs one. They wouldn’t listen to us because the care that patients need, they’re not going to get it, because Prime is trying to squeeze as much juice out of a lemon.” When Mary from RUSH worked as an agency nurse at a unionized hospital, it gave her a glimpse into what conditions might be like. “Nurses wanted to stay and make the hospital a better place to work as opposed to, ‘I’m going to quit and go wherever I feel respected,’ because they do feel respected and appreciated there. Their compensation was on par with other hospitals in the area, and the culture was just more collaborative. Keeping experienced nurses at the bedside was only going to do good things for patients.” Prime Healthcare is a privately held for-profit system, which generates billions of dollars in revenue from its systems across the country, and its assets have only increased since acquiring six more hospitals in the Chicago area. Jesús, who was fired by Prime for advocating for unionization, is directly experiencing their wrath and the wealth they have at their disposal to resist the union. “They have that money. It’s nothing to them because they make billions of dollars off the backs of the patients as well as us.” He continued by saying, “They’re just like, ‘you don’t need any hallway monitors,’ because it just saves them money. They just think, ‘you can take these two patients,’ and they don’t have to pay two nurses. They don’t think about the safety and the potential complications of adverse effects.” Brenda, a nurse at St. Mary, described what provoked nurses to take action. “We decided to go on strike because Prime kept retaliating against our colleagues. They had said that they were going to stop. The day that we received the news of an election date, Prime called two more nurses and left a voicemail that they were terminated because they were, according to Prime, ‘trespassing.’ This was completely false because that’s when we were leafleting, and we had a federal law protecting the right to do that. That’s what made us say, ‘you know what? This is enough.” Richard added, “Our strike was before we had a union, which is unheard of. When our coworkers got fired, a lot of people became very angry. Someone asked me: what was the secret of how you unionized? What was the secret to getting support? The secret to getting support was our company and their war on nurses. A lot of the people became very upset. We won by 96 percent because the company made a lot of nurses very angry.” Even at a so-called non-profit hospital like RUMC, whose policies and practices are nowhere near as nakedly offensive as Prime’s, nurses still overwhelmingly supported unionization. Mary describes how her coworkers saw organizing a union as “having power, having a seat at the table. Having a say in what’s happening to us, what’s happening to our patients. Having a say in our compensation, in our benefits, in our healthcare, in our tuition reimbursement, because that could change whenever Rush wants it. Those benefits could go away at any minute, the only way we can actually secure those is in a contract.” The underlying factor of who ultimately controls the workplace surfaced in both for-profit and non-profit systems. During the unionization campaign, RUMC countered that management had open channels of communication with nurses. Mary described what it looked like: “The hospital’s stance was, ‘We have this great shared governance model. Nurses have so much say. Here are some of the things we’ve taken into account. Here are some of the changes we’ve made.” There was a big push for doing Zoom calls to answer questions, but those questions were very filtered, and we lost our opportunity to talk. Then we lost our cameras. People saw how much Rush was restricting open dialogue, and they were like, “okay.” Jesús described organizing for justice at St. Mary in this way. “It’s a very common issue, and it doesn’t matter what you do, if you’re an Amazon worker or you work in a kitchen, you work. There’s always that power struggle between people trying to make money and you trying to do your job. It’s about the working class coming together.” Brenda reported how workers across different units in the hospital joined together. “It was inspiring how we started to connect unit to unit. Before, ICU [intensive care unit] and emergency room, they are different worlds. In the ICU we’re like, ‘ER is just sending all their patients out to us.’ After getting to know everyone, talking to everyone during the meetings, as well as psychiatry, medical-surgical units… it’s like little towns, right? Getting everyone connected and on the same page, that was one of the best things that we saw.” Jesús went on to describe the importance of links between healthcare workers and their community and how unionization will help stabilize care for patients. “St. Mary has been here a long time. I’ve met people who were like, ‘I was born in this hospital,’ and they have no other place to go, they’re part of the community. Some of them don’t have the pleasure of going to Northwestern or Rush, these fancy hospitals. The community deserves great nurses, but we keep losing nurses to Rush, Northwestern, UIC, and all these other places because St Mary’s cannot compete with them.” Brenda, also from St. Mary, added to this. “With the union, I know that we’re going to get support to fix our staffing grids, and hopefully to retain nurses. Nurses don’t want to do bedside anymore because of the working conditions. During COVID, everyone was a hero, right? All the nurses were heroes. Once that attention went away, they started cutting down. A lot of the things changed about two years ago when Prime took over, and healthcare is now for profit instead of to help our communities.” She further asserted that “healthcare should never bring profit for any company, any government, anything like that. It shouldn’t be a means of profit. In the end, unionization affects our community and affects our patients. With the strike and how much support we had from the community, it was because we’ve taken care of them. We’ve taken care of their kids, we’ve taken care of their families, and themselves. The community knows, and that’s why they were so appreciative and supportive of our movement.” Jesús was one of the multiple nurses that Prime Healthcare had fired during the campaign. Despite this, he shared, “I would still do the exact same thing because regardless of everything that happened, you get further together than just by yourself. We have to organize regardless of where you are, and what you do. At the end of the day you have to work together to make your workplace better. You and your coworkers have a voice which is something that the bosses don’t want you to have.” As was mentioned above, while the 20 percent overall unionization rate of nurses is impressive compared to the average workforce, there is still a lot of room to grow a labor movement of healthcare workers. The overall chronic terrible state of healthcare in this country means there is an ongoing potential to organize patients alongside unions to win significant reforms. A number of newly elected politicians won with a promise of winning healthcare for all. When the Democratic Party majority in Congress gets seated in January 2027, accompanying this event will be severe cuts to Medicaid as a result of Trump’s 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act. These changes will slash about 1 trillion dollars from health services over the next 10 years. Resisting austerity and fighting for the healthcare we deserve will take significant struggle and solidarity between workers and patients – hopefully, the recent victories of nurses in Chicago will help set the stage for successful fights. articles.title: Romania: a growing hub of complicity in genocide
articles.author: Vlad Muresan
articles.content: In April 2026, the opening of yet another Israeli weapons factory in Romania was cause for celebration for some. With great fanfare, Elbit Systems – Israel’s largest private arms manufacturer – inaugurated its seventh production facility in the country, in the small town of Chitila, just outside Bucharest. The company whose weapons have helped sustain Israel’s genocide in Palestine, its decades-long occupation, and its military assaults on Iran was welcomed as a symbol of industrial progress. The event was marked by the test flight of a Watchkeeper X drone and was attended by high ranking Elbit officials, including Uri Maman, VP head of Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) Operations. The chair of the Senate Defense Committee, a former prime minister and defense minister, as well as an adviser to the serving defense minister were also in attendance. The event received extensive coverage across Romania’s major news outlets. Source: Nicoleta Pauliuc/Facebook At the time of the inauguration, the delivery of Romania’s unmanned aerial systems was already approximately ten months overdue. To date, Elbit has yet to deliver any of the contracted drones, with the delay now extending to 16 months. The company has cited force majeure arising from the war to justify this. In previous months, a significant number of similar Elbit drones were downed over Lebanon, Iran and Iraq. Elbit arms Israel’s attacks beyond Palestine. In Lebanon, its munitions were identified in attacks that killed a Reuters journalist and seven relief volunteers . In Syria, its drones conduct surveillance and strikes. In Iran, its armed drones, surveillance and electronic warfare systems supported Israel’s offensive. Through production, procurement and military cooperation, Romania helps sustain an industry that enables Israel’s regional offensives well beyond Gaza and Palestine. Once a socialist state committed to anti-imperialism, Romania has become an important link in the projection of US imperial power across West Asia, serving as both an operating base for US military aircraft and a production and supply hub within Israel’s military-industrial network. A network of complicity Owned by Simultec, one of the three Romanian Elbit Systems subsidiaries, the Chitila factory is the result of a €380 million contract signed by the Romanian state with the company for seven Watchkeeper X unmanned aerial systems. Romanian production of Watchkeeper X drones spans several companies in Elbit’s supply chain: Simultec manufactures composite airframes, A-E Electronics supplies aircraft components, Eurobody Hydraulics produces ground control stations, and Aerostar integrates the drones’ systems. Watchkeeper X presentation in Chitila, Romania. Source: Elbit System In 2024 and 2025, Israel was Romania’s main military export destination. Military equipment and technology worth over €150 million have been shipped from Romania to Israel. Most of these shipments are presumably coming from Elbit’s own Romanian subsidiaries, which are shipping back to Israel military electronics, drone components and mortar systems for integration into weapons platforms. In the first half of 2026, military exports from Romania to Israel amounted to €34 million. Romania authorized €307.24 million in military exports to Israel in 2025 – nearly 99% through global licenses allowing repeated shipments over several years – and a further €53.6 million in the first half of 2026. Romanian military exports to Israel 2025-2026. Source: ANCEX, Romania’s Department for Export Controls, within the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. This newest expansion is symptomatic of a process that has been taking place all across Central and Eastern Europe. Under the guise of rearmament, Israeli companies are moving into the area securing record contracts and expanding their production facilities across the region, with Romania becoming one of its central pillars. Read more: Amid mass protests in the West, Israel’s military footprint expands in Eastern Europe This process further integrates the region into the imperialist world system that enabled the genocide in Gaza, while reinforcing Israel’s impunity and undermining international law and institutions. European rearmament creates new opportunities for complicity European rearmament is opening new markets for Israeli arms manufacturers, including through programmes presented as strengthening Europe’s industrial autonomy. Romania’s allocation of up to €16.68 billion in EU-backed loans under Security Action for Europe (SAFE) illustrates the scale of the opportunity. In May 2026, Romania’s General Aviation Inspectorate awarded a €43.18 million helicopter simulation contract to Simultec under the country’s SAFE investment plan. Although registered locally, the company belongs to the Israeli group. These connections also extend through European suppliers. A separate €30.7 million Romanian SAFE contract covers Vector drones from Germany’s Quantum Systems, whose published specifications identify Israel’s NextVision as the supplier of their electro-optical sensors. NextVision supplies imaging components to Elbit Systems, including for drones deployed in Gaza. In 2025, Norway’s largest pension fund, KLP, excluded the company over the risk that its products contribute to violations of international humanitarian law. Elbit Systems lightweight quadcopter. Source: Flightglobal.com Romania’s planned €3.337 billion SAFE procurement of Rheinmetall’s Lynx infantry fighting vehicles also has Israeli links. The configuration described in news reports incorporates Spike LR2 anti-tank missiles produced in cooperation with Israel’s Rafael Advance Defense Systems. In July 2025, Romania signed a €2.04 billion framework agreement for Rafael’s SPYDER air defense systems, followed by a first implementing contract worth approximately €600 million in June 2026. More Israeli companies moving in Israeli military and surveillance companies are expanding their presence in Romania beyond Elbit. IMCO has opened a component manufacturing facility in Crevedia, while Skylock is pursuing local counter-drone production and SAFE procurement opportunities with Optoelectronica. ParaZero and Aero Sentinel have demonstrated their technologies at Romanian military events and exercises. These are all companies deeply embedded in the Israeli military and responsible for genocide, apartheid and occupation in Palestine. Read more: In Eastern Europe, resistance grows to militarism and Israeli arms production The network also extends into surveillance: Cognyte operates a growing software development centre in Bucharest, while Romanian prosecutors have launched a procurement procedure for Cellebrite phone-extraction tools, whose use against journalists and activists abroad has raised serious human rights concerns. Some Romanians are resisting Elbit Out! is a campaign started in 2025 against a concrete infrastructure of complicity. It targets the fact that Israeli military companies are present in Romania, that they profit in Romania, that they produce in Romania, and that the Romanian government uses public money to strengthen them. Its internationalist approach connects solidarity with Palestine to opposition to the governments, corporations and military partnerships that sustain destruction across the Global South. It brings together struggles against war and austerity, demanding that public resources serve people’s needs. The Elbit Out! campaign published its second report in November 2026. Source: Elbit Out!/Facebook The campaign challenges the system that makes genocide profitable and turns Eastern Europe into a market, production base and source of debt for Western and Israeli weapons manufacturers. In November 2026, Elbit Out! published its second report , documenting how Romania has deepened its ties with Israel’s military-industrial complex through arms exports, public procurement and local weapons production. Released as the campaign enters its second year, the report exposes the growing gap between Romania’s professed commitment to international law and its continued economic and military cooperation with companies implicated in Israel’s crimes in Palestine and across the region.
